title: Solids, liquids and gases: why a gas has mass and fills any container

summary.text: A balloon of air seems to weigh nothing, so does air have mass at all? In this lesson you will weigh two balloons on a hanger to compare gases, watch smoke fill two jars, pour air upwards to catch it, and build a plate of air from 100 grains.
summary.art: A red cooking gas cylinder on a platform scale in an Indian kitchen, with a girl reading the number painted inside its top ring.

intro.hook: A full cooking gas cylinder is 14.2 kilograms heavier than an empty one. You cannot see the gas that burns at the stove. So how can something you cannot see have so much mass?
intro.text: The gas is a real substance, made of particles, just as water and steel are. Its particles are far apart and fly about freely, so we see straight through it. In the cylinder the gas is squeezed until its particles touch, and it becomes a liquid. Air is a gas too, and air has mass. A bedroom holds about 40 kilograms of it. In this lesson you catch a gas, pour it, make a new one, and hang two gases on a balance. You also find out why air seems to weigh nothing at all.
intro.art: A child looking through an empty-looking glass tumbler, with faint dots drawn inside it to show the particles of air.

outcomes: By the end I can show that a gas takes up space and has mass, using my own test results.
By the end I can explain with particles why a gas fills its container. I can also explain why a gas can be squashed but a liquid cannot.
By the end I can compare solids, liquids and gases by shape, volume, flowing and squashing.
By the end I can say what air is made of. I can name four gases around us and what they do.
By the end I can make a gas safely. I can name the state of each thing I started with and of what was made.
By the end I can explain why one gas can be heavier than another. I can also say why a balloon of air seems to weigh nothing.
By the end I can name causes of air pollution in India and say what lowers it. I can also count the dust in the air at home.
By the end I can plan a fair test. I can say what my evidence shows and what it does not show.

terms.meaning: One of the ways a substance can be: solid, liquid or gas. The particles are the same in each state. Only their spacing and movement change.
terms.example: Ice, water and water vapour are three states of the same substance.
terms.art: An ice cube, a tumbler of water and a faint wisp above a kettle spout, side by side.

terms.meaning: A state in which particles touch and are held in place. A solid keeps its own shape and its own volume.
terms.example: A steel spoon stays the same shape in a tumbler, a bowl or your hand.
terms.art: A steel spoon lying in a round bowl, keeping its own shape.

terms.meaning: A state in which particles touch but slide past each other. A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container.
terms.example: One tumbler of buttermilk is still one tumbler when you pour it into a wide bowl.
terms.art: Buttermilk being poured from a tall steel tumbler into a wide bowl.

terms.meaning: A state in which particles are far apart and fly about freely. A gas has no shape or volume of its own. It spreads out to fill its container.
terms.example: The air in a room and the carbon dioxide in a fizzy drink are gases. So is the steam just above a kettle spout.
terms.art: A closed glass jar with a few dots scattered evenly through it and small arrows showing them flying in all directions.

terms.meaning: How much matter a thing is made of. We measure mass in grams and kilograms.
terms.example: One litre of water has a mass of 1 kilogram. One litre of air has a mass of about 1.2 grams.
terms.art: A kitchen scale with a one-litre bottle of water on it, and a small label showing a litre of air beside it.

terms.meaning: How much space a thing takes up. We measure volume in millilitres and litres.
terms.example: A deep breath of a ten-year-old child takes up about one and a half litres.
terms.art: A two-litre bottle with level marks on its side, three-quarters filled with air over water.

terms.meaning: The idea that every solid, liquid and gas is made of tiny moving particles. How close they are and how they move explains how each state behaves.
terms.example: The model explains why you can squash air in a capped bottle but cannot squash water.
terms.art: Three boxes of dots: neat touching rows, jumbled touching dots, and a few far-apart dots with arrows.

terms.meaning: To squash something into a smaller space. Gases can be compressed, because their particles have empty space between them.
terms.example: A cycle pump compresses air into a tyre until the tyre feels hard.
terms.art: A hand pushing down a cycle pump joined to a tyre valve.

terms.meaning: The slow spreading of particles of one substance among the particles of another. It happens because particles move all the time.
terms.example: The smell of jasmine in one corner slowly reaches every part of a closed room.
terms.art: A string of jasmine on a table with dots spreading outwards from it through a room.

terms.meaning: Two or more substances together, each keeping its own particles.
terms.example: Air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen and small amounts of other gases.
terms.art: A plate of rice grains with yellow dal grains mixed evenly among them.

terms.meaning: The gas that makes up about 78 of every 100 particles of air. It has no colour or smell, and our bodies breathe it in and out unchanged.
terms.example: Packets of chips are filled with nitrogen, so the chips stay crisp.
terms.art: A puffed-up packet of chips with a label pointing to the gas inside.

terms.meaning: The gas that makes up about 21 of every 100 particles of air. Humans and other animals need it to get energy from food, and fires need it to burn.
terms.example: Hospitals keep oxygen squeezed into strong steel cylinders.
terms.art: A tall hospital oxygen cylinder beside a bed, with a mask on a tube.

terms.meaning: A gas made when things burn, when living beings breathe out, and when vinegar meets baking soda. It is about one and a half times as heavy as air.
terms.example: The bubbles in soda water are carbon dioxide.
terms.art: A glass of soda water with streams of bubbles rising.

terms.meaning: Water as a gas. It is invisible, and the amount in the air changes from day to day.
terms.example: On a humid monsoon day in Kochi, up to 4 of every 100 particles of air are water vapour.
terms.art: A wet towel on a balcony rail with faint arrows rising from it into the air.

terms.meaning: The lightest gas. It is a gas at room temperature.
terms.example: Weather balloons sent up from Chennai and Thiruvananthapuram are filled with hydrogen, the lightest gas.
terms.art: A round weather balloon rising on a string, with a small label reading hydrogen.

terms.meaning: The layer of air around the Earth. It is thickest near the ground and thins out slowly, with no sharp top.
terms.example: Half of all the air lies below about five and a half kilometres, lower than many Himalayan peaks.
terms.art: The curved edge of the Earth seen from space, with a thin blue glowing layer of air above it.

terms.meaning: How much mass is packed into a certain space. A dense gas is heavy for its size.
terms.example: Carbon dioxide is denser than air, so a balloon of it falls faster than a balloon of air.
terms.art: Two balloons of the same size on a balance, one end lower than the other.

terms.meaning: The upward push of a liquid or a gas on anything inside it. The push equals the weight of the liquid or gas that the thing pushes aside.
terms.example: The upthrust of air holds up a helium balloon, as the upthrust of water holds up a boat.
terms.art: A balloon in the air with a small arrow down for weight and an equal arrow up for upthrust.

terms.meaning: Harmful gases and tiny solid or liquid bits that people add to the air.
terms.example: Smoke from traffic, burning rubbish and wood fires pollutes the air of many Indian cities.
terms.art: A city road at dusk with haze around the street lamps and a bus passing.

terms.meaning: Tiny solid and liquid bits floating in air, each smaller than 2.5 thousandths of a millimetre. They are small enough to go deep into the lungs.
terms.example: A bit of PM2.5 is about thirty times thinner than a human hair.
terms.art: A magnified human hair with a few tiny specks beside it, each far thinner than the hair.

terms.meaning: A number that tells how polluted the air is. In India it runs from 0 to 500. Up to 50 is good, and over 300 is very poor.
terms.example: A weather app may show an AQI of 60 in Thiruvananthapuram and 350 in Delhi on the same winter day.
terms.art: A phone screen showing a coloured AQI dial with a number on it.

explanations.concept: A gas is a substance: it takes up space and has mass
explanations.definition: A gas is matter, just like a solid or a liquid. It is made of particles, it takes up space, and it has mass.
explanations.description: We cannot see most gases, so they are easy to mistake for nothing. Two tests show that a gas is something. First, a gas takes up space. Push a tumbler mouth-down into water, and the air inside keeps the water out. Second, a gas has mass. One litre of air has a mass of about 1.2 grams. That is small, but air adds up. Take a bedroom 4 metres long, 3 metres wide and 3 metres high. The air in it has a mass of about 43 kilograms. When vinegar and baking soda fizz in an open tumbler, the tumbler gets lighter. The lost grams left as carbon dioxide gas. Cooking gas is even sold by mass. A home cylinder holds 14.2 kilograms of it. Some substances are gases at room temperature, which is a normal warm room. Carbon dioxide, hydrogen and water vapour are three of them. Water vapour is water as a gas, and it is in the air on every humid day.
examples: In Pour Air Upwards, air moved from one tumbler to another under water. It pushed the water out of the second tumbler.
In Weigh the Fizz, the open tumbler lost about 3 grams as the gas left. The closed bottle lost nothing until its cap was opened.
An auto-rickshaw driver in Bengaluru buys compressed natural gas by the kilogram.
explanations.art: A kitchen scale showing a tumbler of fizzing liquid, with an arrow of invisible gas leaving and the number on the scale going down.

explanations.definition: A solid keeps its shape and its volume. A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container. A gas keeps neither: it fills all the space it is given.
explanations.description: All three states are made of particles. In a solid the particles touch and are held in place, so they only shake. In a liquid the particles still touch, but they slide past each other, so a liquid flows. In a gas the particles are far apart and fly freely. In the air around you, each particle is about ten of its own widths from the next. That is why a gas can be compressed and the other two cannot. Solids, liquids and gases all have mass. Liquids and gases both flow, so scientists call them both fluids. When water boils, its particles do not grow. They end up about 12 widths apart. So the steam takes about 1,700 times as much space as the water did.
examples: Shape: a steel spoon keeps its shape. Water takes the shape of the tumbler. Air takes the shape of the whole room.
Volume: a litre of milk stays a litre in any vessel. A litre of air let out of a balloon spreads through the room.
Squashing: in The Compare Table, the capped bottle of air squeezed in, and the capped bottle of water did not.
One teaspoon of water, 5 millilitres, boils into about 8.5 litres of steam.
explanations.art: A table with three rows, solid, liquid and gas, and ticks and crosses under the headings keeps shape, keeps volume, flows, can be squashed.

explanations.concept: Why a gas fills its container
explanations.definition: Gas particles fly in straight lines until they hit something, and nothing holds them together. So they keep moving until they are spread through all the space they can reach.
explanations.description: Nothing pushes a gas into the corners of a room. Each particle only flies, hits another particle or a wall, and bounces off in a new direction. With so many particles moving by chance, the spread-out arrangement is far more likely than any other. In the Bean Gas game, six beans moved by the roll of a die. They spread over the whole board and stayed spread. The chance of all six being back in the starting corner at once is 1 in 4,096. A room holds a huge number of particles, a number with 27 digits. With so many, the chance of all of them gathering in one corner is almost zero, so the air never does. Gas particles in air fly at about 500 metres a second. Yet a smell takes a minute or more to cross a still room. Each smell particle hits air particles billions of times a second, so its path zigzags. In a real room, slow air currents carry smells much faster than diffusion alone.
examples: In Smoke in Two Jars, the smoke from one jar spread into both jars and looked thinner in each.
In Still Air or Fan, the smell reached the far chair much sooner with the fan on. Moving air carried it.
Open a bottle of perfume in Mysuru, and by evening some of its particles are streets away.
explanations.art: A room drawn from above with a perfume bottle in one corner and dots spreading out in zigzag paths to every part of the room.

explanations.concept: Compressing a gas, and turning it into a liquid
explanations.definition: A gas can be compressed because there is empty space between its particles. If a gas is compressed and cooled enough, its particles touch, and it becomes a liquid.
explanations.description: Squeeze a capped bottle of air, and its sides go in. The particles have moved closer together. Squeeze a capped bottle full of water, and nothing moves, because its particles already touch. The space between gas particles is truly empty. It is not filled with air, because air is the particles. Cooking gas, called LPG, is compressed until it becomes a liquid. That is how 14.2 kilograms fit in one home cylinder. Let out as a gas at room pressure, it would fill about 7,000 litres. That is as much as 350 buckets of 20 litres. The natural gas in buses and autos, called CNG, is squeezed to about 200 times the pressure of the air. It stays a gas. It would become a liquid only if it were also made very cold.
examples: Rock a full LPG cylinder gently, and you can feel liquid slosh inside. An empty one does not slosh.
A clear plastic lighter shows liquid butane inside. The butane leaves the nozzle as a gas.
A cycle tyre holds air squeezed to between three and five times the pressure of the air outside.
explanations.art: A cut-away drawing of a red LPG cylinder with clear liquid in the lower part, gas above it, and a pipe leading to a blue stove flame.

explanations.concept: One gas can be heavier than another
explanations.definition: At the same temperature and pressure, a litre of any gas holds about the same number of particles. Gases with heavier particles are therefore heavier, litre for litre.
explanations.description: A particle of carbon dioxide has about one and a half times the mass of an average particle of air. So a litre of carbon dioxide has a mass of about 1.8 grams. A litre of air has about 1.2 grams. That is why the carbon dioxide balloon sank lower in Two Balloons on a Hanger. Helium particles are very light. A litre of helium has only about one-seventh of the mass of a litre of air. So a helium balloon rises. A heavy gas can lie at the bottom of a pit or a jug for a while. It sits there like water in a bowl. But its particles keep moving, so in time it mixes with the air above. Leaked LPG is heavier than air and collects near the floor. Piped natural gas is lighter than air and collects near the ceiling.
examples: Carbon dioxide: about 1.8 grams a litre. Air: about 1.2 grams a litre. Helium: about 0.17 grams a litre.
A balloon blown up by mouth falls slowly. A balloon filled with carbon dioxide falls faster.
Weather balloons sent up every day from Chennai and Thiruvananthapuram are filled with hydrogen, the lightest gas.
explanations.art: Three balloons of the same size: one rising on a string, one hanging level, one resting on the floor, labelled helium, air and carbon dioxide.

explanations.concept: Why air seems to weigh nothing
explanations.definition: Anything in air is pushed up by the air around it. The push, called upthrust, equals the weight of the air that the thing pushes aside.
explanations.description: A bag of water held under water feels as if it weighs almost nothing. The water around it holds it up. A balloon of air in a room is the same. The air inside it has a mass of 3 grams or so. But the air around it pushes up with nearly the same force. So a balance in a room shows almost none of that mass. A balance in air shows only how much heavier a thing is than the air it pushes aside. That is why the carbon dioxide balloon showed only its extra mass, about 1 to 2 grams. To weigh air itself, people squeeze extra air into a closed container, or pump the air out of one. The air's weight on us also goes unnoticed, because air pushes on us equally from every side.
examples: In Two Balloons on a Hanger, the air balloon barely moved its end. Yet it held about 3 grams of air.
A football has more mass after pumping, because extra air has been squeezed into the same space.
About 10 tonnes of air rest on every square metre of the ground at sea level.
explanations.art: A girl holding a bag of water under the surface of a bucket of water with one finger, looking surprised at how light it feels.

explanations.definition: Dry air is a mixture of gases. In every 100 particles, about 78 are nitrogen, about 21 are oxygen and about 1 is argon. Carbon dioxide is about 4 particles in every 10,000.
explanations.description: Air also holds water vapour. Desert air has almost none. On a humid day, about 4 in every 100 particles are water vapour. It carries dust, smoke, pollen and spores as well, but these are tiny solids and liquids floating in the gas. Winds stir the atmosphere all the time, and gas particles spread among each other. So the mix of nitrogen and oxygen is almost the same in Chennai, in Shimla and over the sea. What changes with height is how much air there is. At the top of Mount Everest, each breath holds about one-third as many particles as at the seashore. The oxygen in the air was made by living beings. Tiny water-living bacteria began making oxygen more than two thousand million years ago. Plants and algae keep making oxygen now.
examples: In 100 Grains of Air, 78 grains of rice stood for nitrogen and 21 grains of dal for oxygen. One peppercorn stood for argon.
We breathe in air with about 21 parts of oxygen in 100, and breathe out air with about 16.
Carbon dioxide is rare in air, yet plants build their bodies from this gas.
explanations.art: A pie chart of dry air with a large slice for nitrogen, a smaller slice for oxygen and a thin sliver for argon and other gases.

explanations.concept: Air pollution: what we add to the air
explanations.definition: Air pollution is harmful gases and tiny solid or liquid bits that people add to the air. The most harmful bits are the smallest, called PM2.5.
explanations.description: Engines, power stations, factories, burning rubbish, burning crop stubble, firecrackers and building sites all add to it. Indoors, smoke from cooking on wood or dung, mosquito coils and agarbatti add to it too. Because a gas spreads to fill the space it reaches, smoke does not stay where it is made. Large specks of dust are caught by the hairs and wet lining of the nose. PM2.5 is small enough to pass deep into the lungs and even into the blood. Breathing it for years raises the risk of lung and heart disease. In India the Air Quality Index gives one number for the day's air, from 0 to 500. Wind and rain clear the air, and still, cold winter air traps pollution near the ground.
examples: In Five Sticky Squares, the square by the road or the stove usually catches the most specks.
In many villages, the women who cook on wood fires breathe the most smoke in the family. So do the small children near them.
After a heavy monsoon shower in Mumbai, the AQI often falls, because rain washes dust out of the air.
explanations.art: A greased clear plastic square taped beside a window that faces a busy road, with dark specks stuck to it.

explanations.concept: How many states of matter are there?
explanations.description: School books name three states, and three are enough for most things at home. But some things do not fit neatly. Glass is hard like a solid, yet its particles are jumbled like those of a liquid. Toothpaste keeps its shape until you squeeze it, and then it flows. A flame and a lightning flash are plasma, a gas so hot that its particles have broken into charged pieces. Scientists do not agree on one count.
examples: Plasma: lightning, the Sun, and the glow inside a tube light.
Glass: a solid whose particles never lined up in rows.
Carbon dioxide above 31 degrees Celsius and squeezed 73 times is neither a liquid nor a gas. Factories use it to take the caffeine out of coffee.

perspectives.explanation: There are three states: solid, liquid and gas. They explain nearly everything a child meets, and plasma can be added as a fourth.
There are many more states. Plasma, liquid crystals in phone screens and several very cold states each follow their own rules. So each counts as a state.
The states are boxes that people drew. Glass, gels, foams and pastes sit between the boxes, so asking for one exact number is not useful.

explanations.art: Three labelled boxes, solid, liquid and gas, with a pane of glass, a tube of toothpaste and a lightning flash sitting on the lines between them.

agreed.evidence: A closed container gains mass when more gas is pumped in and loses mass when gas is let out. A litre of air at sea level has a mass of about 1.2 grams.

agreed.text: Dry air is about 78 parts nitrogen, 21 parts oxygen and 1 part argon in every 100.
agreed.evidence: Chemists have separated air into its gases and measured each one since the 1770s. Argon was found in 1894, when nitrogen taken from air turned out to be slightly too heavy.

agreed.text: Gas particles are far apart and move fast in all directions.
agreed.evidence: This picture gives the correct sizes for gas pressure, for how gases compress and for how fast they spread. Liquid air takes about 700 times less space than the same air as a gas.
Equal volumes of hydrogen, helium, air and carbon dioxide have been weighed many times. Each gives its own mass, always in the same order.

agreed.text: Tiny bits in polluted air harm the lungs and the heart.
agreed.evidence: Studies have followed many thousands of people for years, in many countries. They find more lung and heart disease where PM2.5 is higher.

agreed.text: The amount of carbon dioxide in the air is rising.
agreed.evidence: It has been measured without a break since 1958 at Mauna Loa in Hawaii. It has risen from about 315 to more than 420 particles in every million.

challenging.claim: Air is nothing, so an empty tumbler is empty.
challenging.who: A common belief, and what our eyes tell us
challenging.for: Air has no colour, smell or taste. A hand moves through it easily, and a tumbler of air pours out nothing we can see.
challenging.against: Air keeps water out of an upturned tumbler. It can be poured upwards under water, squeezed, and weighed when extra air is pumped into a ball.
challenging.context: This card is about the everyday idea that air is nothing at all.

challenging.claim: All gases are light, so every gas rises.
challenging.for: Steam, smoke from a fire and helium balloons all go up. So it seems that going up is what gases do.
challenging.against: Smoke rises because it is hot, and helium because its particles are light. Cold carbon dioxide and leaked LPG are heavier than air and sink to the floor.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that every gas floats upwards.

challenging.claim: Carbon dioxide in the air traps the Sun's heat, so more of it would warm the Earth.
challenging.who: Eunice Newton Foote, an American scientist, in 1856
challenging.for: She filled glass cylinders with different gases and stood them in sunshine. The cylinder of carbon dioxide grew hottest.
challenging.against: Her paper was read out by a man at a science meeting and then forgotten for a very long time. Later measurements by many scientists showed she was right.
challenging.context: This card is about an early finding on carbon dioxide and heat, made by a woman whose work was forgotten.

challenging.claim: Glass is a very slow liquid, which is why old window panes are thicker at the bottom.
challenging.who: A popular belief, repeated in many books
challenging.for: The particles of glass are jumbled like those of a liquid. Some very old window panes really are thicker at the bottom.
challenging.against: In 1998 the physicist Edgar Zanotto did the sums. Window glass would need far longer than the age of the universe to flow that much. Old panes were uneven when they were made.
challenging.context: This card is about whether window glass slowly flows.

challenging.claim: Space begins 100 kilometres above the ground.
challenging.who: The world body that keeps flight records
challenging.for: Above about 100 kilometres the air is too thin for an aeroplane's wings to hold it up. A line is useful for records and for law.
challenging.against: The air has no top edge. It thins out slowly for hundreds of kilometres. Some scientists argue for 80 kilometres instead.
challenging.context: This card is about where the atmosphere ends and space begins.

big_questions.q: A balloon of air on a balance in a room shows almost no weight. So how can we be sure that air has weight?
big_questions.hint: Think about what changes when extra air is squeezed into a football.

big_questions.q: Nobody tells the particles of a gas where to go. Why do they always end up spread through the whole room?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Bean Gas game. How many ways are there to be spread out, and how many to be in one corner?

big_questions.q: Ice, water and steam are made of the same particles. Is 'solid' what a thing is, or what its particles are doing just now?
big_questions.hint: What would you have to change to turn one into another?

big_questions.q: You breathe out carbon dioxide, and a tulsi plant takes that gas in. The plant gives out oxygen, and you breathe that oxygen in. Whose air is it?
big_questions.hint: Follow one particle of carbon dioxide for a day. Where could it go?

big_questions.q: Smoke made in one street spreads to the next street, and to the next town. Who should decide what may be put into the air?
big_questions.hint: Think about who makes the smoke and who breathes it. Are they the same people?

big_questions.q: The air has no sharp top edge. So where does the Earth end?
big_questions.hint: Is the air part of the Earth? Is a satellite inside the Earth's air or outside it?

story.title: The Light Cylinder
story.note: Thenmozhi, Kathir, Selvi athai, Fathima akka, the delivery man and the idli stall are made up. These things are real. A home cooking gas cylinder in India holds 14.2 kilograms of gas. The mass of the empty cylinder is painted on it, and differs a little from one cylinder to the next. The gas is a liquid inside and sloshes when a full cylinder is rocked. A strong smell is added to the gas so that leaks can be noticed. A customer may ask for a cylinder to be weighed when it is delivered. Children should never move or open a gas cylinder.
text: Selvi athai's idli stall stood at the corner of a lane near the Meenakshi temple in Madurai. Every morning before six she lit two big burners under two big steamers. In the school holidays her niece Thenmozhi, who was ten, came to wrap parcels in banana leaf. Thenmozhi's brother Kathir, who was seven, came to eat.

On Thursday the flame under the second steamer shrank to a thin blue ring and went out. Athai stared at it. "Finished? I joined this cylinder on Saturday. A cylinder lasts me twelve days. This one has lasted five."
She shut the knob, took off the regulator and rocked the red cylinder on its base. Nothing moved inside it. "Empty," she said, and rolled the spare cylinder into its place.
"Maybe it leaked," said Kathir.
Athai shook her head. "A leak stinks. They add a smell to the gas so that we can tell. I smelt nothing all week."
"Then maybe they gave you less," said Thenmozhi.
Kathir laughed. "Less gas? How would anyone know? Gas is like air. You can't count air."

Thenmozhi did not answer. She was rocking the spare cylinder, the way Athai had rocked the old one. Something heavy swung inside and slapped the steel, like water in a pot carried on the hip. She rocked the old one. Nothing. "Athai, there is a liquid in the full one."
"Of course there is. They squeeze the gas so hard that it turns into a liquid. It turns back into gas on its way out of the pipe."
"So when the liquid is gone, the cylinder is empty."
"When the liquid is gone, my idlis stop," said Athai, and she went back to her customers.

Thenmozhi crouched beside the old cylinder. Inside the ring at its top, someone had painted a number in white: 15.8. On the spare one the paint said 16.1. "Kathir, why would they paint a number on each cylinder? And why are the two numbers different?"
"Roll numbers," said Kathir, with his mouth full.
"Roll numbers don't have points in them." She looked at the bill clipped to the wall. Net weight: 14.2 kg. She read it twice. "Kathir. They sell the gas by the kilo. Like rice."
"You can't weigh gas."

"They do. Fourteen point two kilos. So the number on the ring must be the cylinder alone, with nothing in it. No two cylinders are made exactly alike, so each has its own number." She stood up. "Then we can find out what is inside this spare one without opening it."
Fathima akka's rice shop next door had a platform scale for sacks. Akka laughed at the idea, but she helped them roll the old cylinder onto the scale first. The red numbers settled at 15.9.
"Wrong," said Kathir. "The paint says fifteen point eight."

Thenmozhi frowned at the 15.9 for a long moment. "It isn't wrong. The liquid is gone, but the cylinder is still full of gas. It is gas that isn't squeezed any more. It fills the whole inside, and it weighs a hundred grams."
"A hundred grams of nothing," said Kathir, but he said it quietly.

Then they rolled the spare cylinder on. Athai had come to the door, wiping her hands on her sari. Thenmozhi did the sum aloud before she looked. "Sixteen point one for the steel. Fourteen point two for the gas. It should say thirty point three."
The scale said 25.1.

Nobody spoke. Akka bent down to check that nothing was touching the platform. Thenmozhi wrote the numbers on the back of a parcel wrapper. "Twenty-five point one, take away sixteen point one. Nine kilos of gas. They sold you fourteen point two, Athai. Five point two kilos are missing."
"And the old one finished in five days," Athai said slowly. "In eleven years I never once asked them to weigh a cylinder. The delivery men are supposed to carry a scale. I thought, who weighs gas?"

When the delivery man came, he did not argue. He hung the spare cylinder from his own spring scale and read the same number. He said a half-used cylinder that someone had sent back must have been loaded with the full ones. He brought a new cylinder from the lorry and weighed it where everyone could see. The paint said 15.5. The scale said 29.7.
"Fifteen point five and fourteen point two," said Kathir, before anyone else could. "Twenty-nine point seven. This one is honest."

After the lorry had gone, Kathir climbed onto Akka's scale himself. Twenty-two kilos. He filled his cheeks and blew a long breath down at the platform. The numbers did not move. "My breath weighs nothing," he said. "So I was right about that."

"Your breath didn't stay on the scale," said Thenmozhi. "It went off into the lane the moment it left your mouth. Gas goes everywhere it can. If you want to weigh it, you have to catch it in something closed first."
Kathir looked at the red cylinder, and then down the lane, where his breath had gone. "That's why they need all that steel," he said.
Athai lifted the lid of the steamer, and a white cloud rolled up into the morning. She put a hot idli on a leaf for each of them. "Eat," she said. "These were cooked on gas that my niece weighed."
story.epiphany: For the parent: a gas has mass, so cooking gas is sold by the kilogram. A home cylinder holds 14.2 kilograms, and the mass of the empty steel cylinder is painted on it. So the gas inside can be found by weighing the cylinder and taking away the painted number. In the cylinder the gas is squeezed into a liquid. When the liquid is used up, the cylinder is still full of gas at low pressure. That gas has a mass of about 100 grams. A gas let loose spreads out at once. So it must be caught in a closed container before it can be weighed.
ask: Kathir said nobody can count or weigh gas. What on the bill showed that gas is sold by mass?
Why is a number painted on every cylinder, and why does it differ from one cylinder to the next?
The old cylinder had no liquid left, yet the scale showed 100 grams more than the painted number. What was still inside?
Why did Kathir's breath not change the number on the scale?
What would you weigh, and what sum would you do, to check a cylinder at your home?

roots.context: We have learned that a gas is a substance with mass, and that it fills its container. We have also learned that air is a mixture of gases. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In Two Balloons on a Hanger, a balloon full of air hardly moved the hanger. Yet it held about 3 grams of air. The air around it pushed it up by almost as much. So a balance in a room shows only how much heavier a thing is than the air around it.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'as light as air', and we call a tumbler of air empty. We do so because air shows no weight in our hands. Air seems weightless only because we weigh everything while standing inside air. The weight is there, and the surrounding air hides it.
deep_truth.evidence: In Two Balloons on a Hanger, the air balloon against a flat balloon left the hanger almost level. The carbon dioxide balloon showed only its extra mass, 1 to 2 grams more than the air balloon. In Weigh the Fizz, a closed bottle kept its mass until the gas was let out. A bag of water held under water shows the same thing: the water around it holds it up.

three.who_am_i: You take in about 6 litres of air every minute, and about 10 kilograms of it in a day. That is more than three times the mass of all your food and drink.
three.what_is_life: A tree builds their trunk mostly from carbon dioxide, which is a gas in the air. The carbon in wood came out of that carbon dioxide, one particle at a time.
three.what_is_this_world: The space between things is full of gas. About 10 tonnes of air rest on every square metre of the ground. We live at the bottom of this layer of air.

roots.thread: Ice, water and steam look like three different things, and they are one kind of particle moving in three ways. Air looks like nothing, and it is several gases mixed evenly around the whole Earth. The same particles of oxygen and carbon dioxide pass through leaves, lungs, fires and seas, again and again. A gas spreads into all the space it can reach. So no room and no country has air of its own. One layer of air is shared by every being that breathes.

teachings.source: Chandogya Upanishad 4.3.1 to 4.3.2, the teaching of Raikva
teachings.teaching: Raikva calls air the one that takes everything in. He says that when a fire goes out, the fire goes into the air. He says that when water dries up, the water goes into the air.
teachings.link: This matches what the science finds for these two cases. Water that dries up does go into the air, as water vapour. What a fire makes also goes into the air, as carbon dioxide and water vapour.

teachings.source: Anaximenes of Miletus, about 550 BCE, as reported by later Greek writers
teachings.teaching: Anaximenes taught that everything is made of air. Thinned out, air becomes fire. Packed closer, it becomes wind, then cloud, then water, then earth and stone.
teachings.link: He was wrong that everything is air. But he saw that one substance can be thin or thick, flowing or hard. It depends on how closely it is packed. That is close to how particles explain gas, liquid and solid.

teachings.teaching: Yajnavalkya says that air is the thread. By air, as by a thread, this world and all beings are strung together.
teachings.link: The science does not prove this teaching. It does show one plain thing: every breathing being takes from, and gives to, the same mixed air.
verse: वायुना वै गौतम सूत्रेणायं च लोकः परश्च लोकः सर्वाणि च भूतानि संदृब्धानि भवन्ति

science.text: Gases have mass. The atmosphere presses on the ground with the weight of about 10 tonnes on each square metre.
Living beings made the oxygen in the air. The carbon in living bodies came from the carbon dioxide in the air.
How many states of matter there are depends on how they are counted. Scientists do not agree on one number.

other_view.who: Materialists, such as the Charvaka school of ancient India and many scientists today
other_view.view: Only matter is real, and air is matter moving by chance. It joins beings together no more than a road joins the people who walk on it. Sharing air is a fact about gases, and it carries no deeper meaning.

practice.title: Feel one breath arrive and leave
practice.say: Let's sit still and hold one hand just below the nose. Breathe in slowly. Feel the cool air come in. Breathe out slowly. Feel the warm air on your hand. Each breath is about a third of a litre of gas. Now let's take six slow breaths. With each one, notice where the air goes after it leaves you.
practice.kid: Sit still. Hold one hand just below your nose. Breathe in slowly. The air feels cool. Breathe out slowly. The air feels warm on your hand. Take six slow breaths. Where does the air go after it leaves you?

ask: The air you breathed out a minute ago is spreading through this room. When does it stop being your breath?
A fish lives inside water all the time. We live inside air all the time. What else might we be living inside without noticing?
Air belongs to nobody, and everybody needs it. Who should look after it?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged by an open window with one hand held below her nose, and faint dots of air drifting between her, a tulsi plant and the sky outside.

games.title: Solid, Liquid, Gas, or a Mix of States?
games.context: This is a card game about the states of matter. You read a card and decide its state: solid, liquid, gas or a mix of states. Then you give a reason.

printables.title: 24 state cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A steel tumbler
items.b: Solid. It keeps its own shape and its own volume.

items.f: Rice poured from a dabba
items.b: Solid. Each grain keeps its own shape. A heap pours because the grains roll over each other.

items.f: An ice cube just out of the freezer
items.b: Solid. Its water particles are held in place, in neat rows.

items.f: A camphor tablet
items.b: Solid. It keeps its shape, though it slowly turns straight into a gas.

items.f: A rubber band
items.b: Solid. It stretches, but it keeps its volume and springs back.

items.f: A pane of window glass
items.b: Solid. It keeps its shape, though its particles are jumbled like those of a liquid.

items.f: Coconut oil on a hot afternoon in Chennai
items.b: Liquid. It flows and takes the shape of its bottle. On a cool night it sets into a solid.

items.f: Honey
items.b: Liquid. It flows slowly, but it still takes the shape of its jar.

items.f: The cooking gas inside a full cylinder
items.b: Liquid. The gas has been compressed until its particles touch.

items.f: Petrol in a scooter tank
items.b: Liquid. It keeps its volume and takes the shape of the tank.

items.f: Melted wax round a burning candle wick
items.b: Liquid. Heat has freed the wax particles to slide past each other.

items.f: Mercury in an old thermometer
items.b: Liquid. A metal that flows at room temperature.

items.f: The air in a cycle tyre
items.b: Gas. It is compressed, and it fills the whole tyre.

items.f: Steam just above a kettle spout, where nothing can be seen
items.b: Gas. Water vapour is invisible.

items.f: Helium in a floating balloon
items.b: Gas. It fills the balloon, and it is much lighter than air.

items.f: The nitrogen in a packet of chips
items.b: Gas. It fills the packet and keeps the chips from being crushed.

items.f: Cooking gas at the burner, just before it burns
items.b: Gas. Out of the cylinder, the liquid has turned back into a gas.

items.f: The oxygen you are breathing in now
items.b: Gas. About 21 of every 100 particles of air are oxygen.

items.f: Fog on a winter morning in Delhi
items.b: A mix of states. Tiny drops of liquid water float in a gas, the air.

items.f: Smoke from an agarbatti
items.b: A mix of states. Tiny solid and liquid bits float in a gas, the air.

items.f: Soda water in a bottle that was just opened
items.b: A mix of states. A gas is dissolved in a liquid, and comes out as bubbles.

items.f: A bath sponge
items.b: A mix of states. A soft solid full of holes, and the holes hold a gas, the air.

items.f: The foam on a tumbler of filter coffee
items.b: A mix of states. Bubbles of gas, each inside a thin wall of liquid.

items.f: The white cloud above a boiling kettle
items.b: A mix of states. Tiny drops of liquid water float in the air. The steam itself is invisible.

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, with the name of the thing facing up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say which state the thing is in, and give one reason.
A reason must use a property: shape, volume, flowing or squashing.
Turn the card over. If your state and your reason were right, keep the card. If not, put the card on its space on the mat.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most cards wins.
Playing alone: try to keep all 24 cards, then play again to beat your score.

setup.art: A table with a pile of cards and a paper mat with four spaces labelled Solid, Liquid, Gas and A mix of states.
setup.caption: 1. Put the pile of cards next to the mat.

setup.art: A girl holding up a card that says 'Fog on a winter morning' and pointing at the space marked A mix of states.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card, say the state and give a reason.

setup.art: The same card turned over to show the answer written on its back.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over to check.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 cards and the mat. 2. Shuffle the cards. 3. Put them in a pile, with the name of the thing facing up.
flow.say: Some things are a solid, a liquid or a gas. Some are two states mixed together. Let's see if we can tell which.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and the mat. Mix the cards. Put them in a pile.
flow.context: This is the first step of Solid, Liquid, Gas, or a Mix of States? Here you set up the cards and the mat.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read the top card. 2. Say the state and one reason. 3. Turn the card over to check.
flow.say: Read the card aloud. Which state is it in? What property tells you so?
flow.kid: Read the card. Say solid, liquid, gas or a mix. Say why. Then turn it over.

ask.q: Rice pours like water. Why is it a solid?
good: Each grain keeps its own shape.
Only the heap flows, because the grains roll.

flow.parent: A good reason names a property. 'Because it is wet' is not a reason, so ask what the thing does to its shape and its volume.
flow.context: This is the main part of Solid, Liquid, Gas, or a Mix of States? Here you read each card, name the state and give a reason.

flow.do: 1. Count your cards. 2. Look at the cards on the mat together. 3. Talk about the ones that surprised you.
flow.say: Which cards went on the mat? What fooled us about them?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Which thing surprised you most? Why?

check.q: The white cloud above a boiling kettle can be seen. What is it?
options: Water as a gas
Tiny drops of liquid water floating in air
Smoke from the kettle
check.why: Water as a gas is invisible. The white cloud forms where the hot vapour cools and turns into tiny drops of liquid. Choosing 'water as a gas' mixes up steam with the mist it turns into.

flow.context: This is the last step of Solid, Liquid, Gas, or a Mix of States? Here you count your cards and talk about the surprises.

games.title: Bean Gas: do six beans fill the box?
games.context: This is a dice game. Six beans stand for particles of a gas let out in one corner of a box. Each bean moves by the roll of a die, and you watch whether the gas fills the box.

printables.title: A board to draw: a square of 16 small squares
items: Draw a big square with 4 rows of 4 small squares, each about 4 cm wide.
Draw a thick line round the outside. These are the walls of the box.
Draw a thick line across the middle and another down the middle. They split the board into 4 quarters of 4 squares each.
Write START in the small square at the top left corner.

printables.title: A key for the die
items: Roll 1: the bean moves one square up.
Roll 2: the bean moves one square down.
Roll 3: the bean moves one square left.
Roll 4: the bean moves one square right.
Roll 5 or 6: the bean stays on the same square.

printables.title: A score sheet
items: My guess: how many rounds until every quarter holds a bean?
Tally of rounds played until every quarter held a bean:
Ten more rounds: the number of beans in the START quarter after each round:

rules: You need the board, one die and 6 dry beans of the same kind, such as rajma or chana.
Put all 6 beans on the START square. This is a gas let out in one corner of a box.
In one round, roll the die once for each bean and move that bean by the key.
If a move would take a bean off the board, the bean has hit a wall. That bean stays on the same square. Any number of beans may share a square.
After each round, make a tally mark. The gas has filled the box when every quarter holds at least one bean.
Then play 10 more rounds. After each round, write how many beans are in the START quarter.
With friends: each player has a board and a die. The player whose gas fills the box in the fewest rounds wins. Alone: play three games and compare your scores.

setup.art: A hand-drawn board of sixteen squares on paper, split into four quarters by thick lines, with six rajma beans heaped on the top left square.
setup.caption: 1. Put all 6 beans on START.

setup.art: A child rolling a die beside the board and sliding one bean one square to the right.
setup.caption: 2. Roll once for each bean and move that bean by the key.

setup.art: The same board with the six beans scattered, at least one in every quarter.
setup.caption: 3. The gas has filled the box when every quarter holds a bean.

flow.do: 1. Draw the board and copy the key. 2. Put the 6 beans on START. 3. Ask for two guesses. How many rounds until every quarter holds a bean? Will all 6 beans ever be back in the START quarter?
flow.say: Nobody will tell these beans where to go. The die decides. Will they spread over the whole board? Will they ever all come back to the START quarter?
flow.kid: Draw the board. Put 6 beans on START. Make your two guesses.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bean Gas. Here you set up the board and guess what the beans will do.

flow.do: 1. Play round after round. 2. Make a tally mark after each round. 3. Stop when every quarter holds at least one bean.
flow.say: Roll for each bean in turn. Is any bean being sent towards the empty quarters, or do they just wander?
flow.kid: Roll the die for each bean. Move that bean by the key. Make a tally mark after each round. Stop when every quarter holds a bean.
flow.parent: It usually takes between 8 and 26 rounds, most often about 14. That is about ten minutes of rolling.
flow.context: This is the main part of Bean Gas. Here you roll the die for each bean until the beans have spread into every quarter.

flow.do: 1. Play 10 more rounds. 2. After each one, write how many beans are in the START quarter. 3. Ask whether the beans ever all went back, and why not.
flow.say: Look at your ten numbers. The beans were free to go back to START at any time. Why did they not all go back together?
flow.kid: Play 10 more rounds. Count the beans in the START quarter each time.
flow.parent: The START quarter usually holds 1 or 2 beans, sometimes none or 3. Each bean has 1 chance in 4 of being there. The chance that all 6 are there at once is 1 in 4,096. Real gas particles also move by chance. A room holds so many that its air never gathers in one corner.

check.q: In Bean Gas, no bean was told where to go. Why did the beans end up spread over the board?
options: The walls pushed the beans apart
Chance moves give many more spread-out arrangements than gathered ones
The die sends beans to the far corner
check.why: Each bean only wanders. But six beans can be spread out in thousands of ways. They can all sit in one quarter in very few ways. So chance alone spreads them, and keeps them spread. A gas fills its container in the same way.

flow.context: This is the last step of Bean Gas. Here you check whether the beans stay spread out once they have filled the box.

experiments.title: Two Balloons on a Hanger: is one gas heavier than another?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make carbon dioxide gas from vinegar and baking soda, and catch it in a balloon. Then you hang it on a coat-hanger balance beside a balloon of air of the same size.
experiments.question: Does a balloon full of air pull a balance down? Two balloons are the same size. One is full of air and one is full of carbon dioxide. Which is heavier?
experiments.predict: Guess twice, and write both guesses. First: a balloon blown up with air hangs opposite a flat balloon. Which end of the hanger goes down, or does it stay level? Second: a balloon of air hangs opposite a balloon of carbon dioxide of the same size. Which end goes down? Why do you think so, each time?
experiments.fair_test: Use two balloons from the same packet. Make them the same size by measuring round each one with a thread. Hang them the same distance from the middle of the hanger. Switch off the fan and close the windows, because moving air pushes balloons about. Then swap the two balloons and test again, in case one end of the hanger is heavier.
results_table: What hung on the two ends
Paper clips needed to level it

materials.item: round balloons from the same packet (one is a spare)
an empty, dry one-litre plastic bottle
white vinegar
materials.qty: 150 ml, which is three-quarters of a 200 ml tumbler

materials.item: baking soda (cooking soda, not baking powder)
a sheet of paper rolled into a funnel
a coat hanger, and a door handle, hook or nail to hang it from
sewing thread, scissors and sticky tape
a ruler and a pencil
small paper clips or small safety pins

experiments.safety: A grown-up helps to fit the balloon on the bottle. Keep faces away from the bottle mouth, and rinse with water if vinegar gets in an eye. Never put a balloon of this gas to your mouth. Keep balloons away from children under three.

schedule.what: Make the hanger balance. Test a balloon of air. Make carbon dioxide in a balloon. Hang the two balloons, swap them, and race them to the floor.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Show which end of the hanger was lower. Draw it, or take a photo. Then write what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how far one end of the hanger dropped
example_chart.x: What hung on the two ends

data.label: Carbon dioxide balloon and air balloon

example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A coat hanger hanging from a door handle, with a flat balloon tied by a thread to each end and a pencil mark on a paper behind one end.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a flat balloon from each end of a hanger, and mark where one end sits.

setup.art: A one-litre plastic bottle with vinegar in the bottom and a balloon stretched over its mouth, swelling as the liquid fizzes.
setup.caption: 2. Tip baking soda from the balloon into the vinegar. The gas fills the balloon.

setup.art: A hand measuring round a blown-up balloon with a piece of thread.
setup.caption: 3. Make the air balloon the same size as the gas balloon.

setup.art: The hanger with a blown-up balloon at each end, one end clearly lower than the other, and a ruler held upright beside it.
setup.caption: 4. Hang both balloons and measure which end is lower.

flow.do: 1. Hang the coat hanger on a door handle or hook, away from the fan. 2. Tie a 30 cm thread to each end of the hanger. 3. Tie one flat balloon to each thread by its neck. 4. If one end is lower, stick small bits of tape on the higher end until the hanger is level. 5. Tape a sheet of paper behind one end and mark where that end sits.
flow.say: We are going to weigh gases. First we need a balance. This hanger must sit level with a flat balloon on each end.
flow.kid: Hang the hanger on a door handle. Tie a flat balloon to each end. Is it level? Add tape to the higher end. Mark where one end sits.
flow.parent: Switch off the fan and close the windows now. Even a small draught swings the balloons. Tie the threads with bows, because the balloons come off and go back on.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Balloons on a Hanger. Here you turn a coat hanger into a balance and check that it is level.

flow.do: 1. Ask for the first guess and its reason. 2. Untie one balloon. Blow it up, by mouth or with a pump, until it is about 50 cm round, and knot it. 3. Hang it back on its thread. 4. Wait until the hanger is still. 5. Measure how far the end has moved from the pencil mark.
flow.say: One balloon will be full of air and the other flat. Which end will go down, or will the hanger stay level? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Blow up one balloon. Hang it back on its thread. Wait until it is still. Look at the mark.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Air has mass, so the full balloon should go down.
Balloons float, so the full one might go up.
Air weighs nothing, so nothing will change.

flow.parent: Most hangers stay level, or the full end dips by a few millimetres. Do not explain yet. Just ask your child to write what they saw. The reason comes in the last step.
flow.context: This step of Two Balloons on a Hanger tests one balloon full of air against a flat balloon.

flow.do: 1. Show the vinegar, the baking soda and the bottle. 2. Say that they will make a gas called carbon dioxide, and that the gas will fill the third balloon. 3. Ask for the second guess and its reason. 4. Write both guesses down.
flow.say: Next we fill a balloon with a different gas, and make it the same size as the air balloon. Which of the two will be heavier, or will they match? Why?
flow.kid: A new gas will go in the other balloon. Both balloons will be the same size. Write your guess down.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: They are the same size, so they should weigh the same.
Gas weighs nothing, so the hanger will stay level.
The new gas might be heavier, because it is a different substance.

flow.context: This step of Two Balloons on a Hanger is for guessing. You guess whether a balloon of carbon dioxide is heavier than a balloon of air.

flow.do: 1. Pour 150 ml of vinegar into the dry bottle. 2. Use the paper funnel to put 3 level teaspoons of baking soda into a flat balloon. 3. Stretch the balloon's neck over the bottle mouth, with the balloon hanging to one side. 4. Hold the neck on tightly. Lift the balloon, and shake the soda down a little at a time. 5. Swirl the bottle gently until the fizzing stops, in about 2 minutes.
flow.say: Vinegar is a liquid, and baking soda is a solid. Watch what happens when they meet. What is filling the balloon?
flow.kid: Put the soda in the balloon. Fit the balloon on the bottle. Tip the soda in slowly. Watch the balloon grow.

ask.q: We began with a liquid and a solid. What state is the new substance in the balloon?
good: A gas.
It is carbon dioxide, a new gas made when the two met.

flow.parent: Tip the soda in slowly, so that foam does not climb into the balloon. The balloon usually grows to 15 to 18 cm across. A smaller balloon still works. If you can see liquid inside the balloon, start again with the spare, because drops of liquid would add mass.
flow.context: This step of Two Balloons on a Hanger makes carbon dioxide gas from vinegar and baking soda. The gas is caught in a balloon.

flow.do: 1. Pinch the balloon's neck and twist it three times. 2. Lift it off the bottle and tie it. 3. Wrap a thread round the widest part of this balloon and cut the thread to that length. 4. Blow up a fresh balloon with air until the same thread just fits round it, and knot it.
flow.say: For a fair test, the two balloons must be the same size. Blow up a fresh air balloon until the thread just fits round it.
flow.kid: Tie the gas balloon. Measure round it with a thread. Blow up a new air balloon just as big. Now only the gas is different.
flow.parent: A balloon blown by mouth is fine. Breath is almost the same mixture as air. Put the first air balloon aside. It was only a rough size, and the new one matches the gas balloon.
flow.context: This step of Two Balloons on a Hanger makes the air balloon and the carbon dioxide balloon the same size.

flow.do: 1. Take the old balloons off the threads. Tie the gas balloon to one thread and the matching air balloon to the other. 2. Wait until the hanger is still. 3. Hold the ruler upright and measure how far the lower end is below the pencil mark's level. 4. Swap the two balloons to the other ends, and measure again. 5. Hook paper clips onto the thread of the higher balloon, one at a time, until the hanger is level. Count them.
flow.say: Which end is lower? Now swap the balloons over. Does the same balloon go down again?
flow.kid: Hang both balloons. Wait until they are still. Which end is lower? Measure it. Swap the balloons and look again. Add paper clips to level it.
flow.parent: The carbon dioxide end usually sits 1 to 3 cm lower. It takes 2 to 4 small paper clips to level the hanger. A small paper clip has a mass of about half a gram. If you see no difference, check for a draught, and check that the gas balloon did not leak.
flow.context: This step of Two Balloons on a Hanger hangs the two balloons on the balance. You swap them over and measure the difference.

flow.do: 1. Untie both balloons. 2. Hold one in each hand, as high as you can reach, at the same height. 3. Let go of both at the same moment. 4. Do this three times and note which lands first each time.
flow.say: Here is a second test of the same question. Let both balloons go together. Which one reaches the floor first?
flow.kid: Hold both balloons up high, at the same height. Let go together. Which lands first? Do it three times.
flow.context: This step of Two Balloons on a Hanger drops the two balloons together, as a second way to compare them.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your results. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The two balloons were the same size. Why was one heavier?
good: Carbon dioxide particles are heavier than the particles of air.
The same space holds about the same number of particles, so heavier particles make a heavier balloon.

ask.q: The air balloon held about 3 grams of air. Why did the hanger not show it?
good: The balloon was hanging in air, and the air around it held it up.
A bag of water under water feels light for the same reason.

flow.parent: Both gases have mass. A litre of air has a mass of about 1.2 grams. A litre of carbon dioxide has about 1.8 grams, because its particles are heavier. The air balloon held about 3 grams of air. But the air around it pushed it up by nearly the same amount, so the hanger hardly showed it. The hanger showed only how much heavier the carbon dioxide is than the air it pushed aside. That is 1 to 2 grams.
flow.think: How could you weigh the air in a balloon, if a balance in a room does not show it?

check.q: In Two Balloons on a Hanger, the carbon dioxide balloon sank lower than the air balloon. Both were the same size. What does that show?
options: Air has no mass at all
Carbon dioxide is heavier than air, litre for litre
The carbon dioxide balloon held a liquid
check.why: Both gases have mass, and carbon dioxide has more of it in the same space. Choosing 'air has no mass' forgets that the air balloon was held up by the air around it. The balloon held only gas: a balloon with liquid in it would not be a fair test.

flow.context: This is the last step of Two Balloons on a Hanger. Here you explain why the carbon dioxide balloon was heavier, and why the air balloon added almost nothing.

experiments.title: Weigh the Fizz: does the gas that leaves have mass? (if you have a kitchen scale)
experiments.context: In this experiment you fizz vinegar and baking soda on a kitchen scale. You do it once in an open tumbler and once in a closed bottle. You watch whether the mass changes as the gas leaves. You need a kitchen scale that shows single grams.
experiments.question: When vinegar and baking soda fizz, does the mass on the scale change? Does it matter whether the gas can escape?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Vinegar and baking soda will fizz in an open tumbler on a scale. Will the number go up, go down or stay the same? Then the same amounts will fizz in a closed bottle. What will the number do this time? Why do you think so? Write both guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same amounts both times: 100 ml of vinegar and 2 level teaspoons of baking soda. Weigh everything together, before and after, on the same scale. Only one thing changes: whether the gas can get out.

materials.item: a kitchen scale that shows single grams
white vinegar
baking soda (cooking soda)
a tall steel tumbler, a small katori, a teaspoon and a steel plate with a rim
an empty fizzy-drink bottle of 1.25 to 2 litres, with its cap
a small piece of tissue paper, about 10 cm square

experiments.safety: Use only a plastic fizzy-drink bottle for the closed test. Never use a glass bottle or a thin water bottle. A grown-up closes and opens the cap. Open it slowly, pointing away from faces.

schedule.what: Weigh an open tumbler before and after the fizz. Then weigh a closed bottle before the fizz, after the fizz and after opening the cap.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

setup.art: A kitchen scale with a rimmed steel plate on it, and on the plate a tumbler of vinegar and a small katori of white powder.
setup.caption: 1. Weigh the plate, the vinegar and the baking soda together.

setup.art: The same tumbler fizzing over a little onto the plate, with the number on the scale lower than before.
setup.caption: 2. Tip the soda in. Watch the number while it fizzes.

setup.art: A closed two-litre plastic bottle fizzing inside, standing on the scale.
setup.caption: 3. Do it again in a closed bottle. Read the scale before and after you open the cap.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the scale, the vinegar and the baking soda. 2. Ask for both guesses and the reasons. 3. Write them down.
flow.say: The mix will fizz on the scale, first in an open tumbler and then in a closed bottle. What will the number do each time? Why?
flow.kid: The mix will fizz on the scale. Will the number go up, down or stay? What about in a closed bottle? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Weigh the Fizz. Here you guess what the scale will show when a fizzing mix loses its gas.

flow.do: 1. Put the plate on the scale, and stand the tumbler and the katori on the plate. 2. Pour 100 ml of vinegar into the tumbler. 3. Put 2 level teaspoons of baking soda in the katori. 4. Write down the mass. 5. Tip the soda into the vinegar, and put the katori back on the plate. 6. Swirl the tumbler once the foam drops, and put it back. After 3 minutes, write down the mass again.
flow.say: Everything stays on the scale: the plate, the katori and any drops that splash. Watch the number while it fizzes.
flow.kid: Put the plate, tumbler, vinegar and soda on the scale. Write the number. Tip the soda in. Watch the number. Write it again after 3 minutes.

ask.q: Nothing was taken off the scale. So where did the missing grams go?
good: They left as gas.
The bubbles carried mass away into the air.

flow.parent: The mass usually falls by about 3 grams, somewhere between 2 and 4. The plate catches any splashes, so the lost mass can only be gas.
flow.context: This step of Weigh the Fizz weighs an open tumbler of vinegar and baking soda before and after the fizz.

flow.do: 1. Pour 100 ml of vinegar into the fizzy-drink bottle. 2. Wrap 2 level teaspoons of baking soda in the tissue and twist it shut. 3. Put the bottle, its cap and the packet on the scale. Write down the mass. 4. Drop the packet into the bottle and screw the cap on tight at once. 5. Swirl the bottle until the fizzing stops, and put it back on the scale. Write down the mass. 6. Open the cap slowly, wait one minute, and weigh the bottle and cap again.
flow.say: This time the gas cannot get out. What does the scale say after the fizz? Now listen as I open the cap, and read the scale again.
flow.kid: Fizz the mix in the closed bottle. Read the scale. Did the number change? Now open the cap slowly. Listen. Read the scale again.
flow.parent: With the cap on, the mass stays the same to the gram, and the bottle goes hard. When the cap opens you hear the gas rush out, and the mass usually falls by 2 to 3 grams. Some carbon dioxide stays in the bottle, so the fall may be a little smaller than in the tumbler.
flow.context: This step of Weigh the Fizz does the same fizz in a closed bottle. You weigh it before and after the cap is opened.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your numbers. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Why did the closed bottle keep its mass while it fizzed?
good: The gas was still inside the bottle.
Nothing could leave, so no mass was lost.

ask.q: A litre of carbon dioxide has a mass of about 1.8 grams. About how many litres of gas left the tumbler?
good: If 3 grams left, a little under 2 litres.

flow.parent: The fizz makes carbon dioxide, and a gas has mass. In the open tumbler the gas left, and its mass left the scale with it. In the closed bottle the gas stayed, so the mass stayed. This is how chemists first learned to keep track of gases: by weighing before and after.

check.q: In Weigh the Fizz, the open tumbler lost about 3 grams. The closed bottle lost none until it was opened. Why?
options: The gas has mass, and it left the open tumbler
Fizzing destroys a little matter
The closed bottle did not fizz
check.why: Matter is not destroyed in a fizz. The missing grams are the carbon dioxide that went into the air. In the closed bottle the same gas was made, but it stayed inside, so the scale did not change.

flow.context: This is the last step of Weigh the Fizz. Here you explain why the open tumbler lost mass and the closed bottle did not.

experiments.title: Still Air or Fan: what carries a smell across a room?
experiments.context: In this experiment a strong smell is let out at one end of a closed room. You time how long it takes to reach your nose 3 metres away. You do this first in still air and then with the fan on.
experiments.question: How long does a smell take to cross 3 metres of still air? Does it arrive sooner or later when a fan is on? Does it reach every part of the room?
experiments.predict: Guess first. How many seconds will the smell take to reach you in still air? With the fan on, will it arrive sooner, later or never? Why do you think so? Write your guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same room, the same chair 3 metres from the smell, and the same amount of smell each time. Rest your nose in another room between the two runs. Only one thing changes: whether the fan is on.
results_table: Seconds until the first smell at 3 metres
Smell in the far corner after 5 minutes? (yes or no)

materials.item: a strong smell: two puffs of perfume or deodorant on a cotton ball, or a dab of pain balm
a small steel dabba with a lid
a phone timer, a measuring tape and a chair
a room with a ceiling fan or a table fan, and a door and windows that close

experiments.safety: Spray the perfume onto the cotton outside the room, away from faces. Do not use this test if anyone at home gets asthma or headaches from strong smells.

schedule.what: Time the smell in still air. Air the room for 5 minutes. Time the smell again with the fan on.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

setup.art: A closed room seen from above, with a small steel dabba on a stool at one end and a child on a chair 3 metres away with eyes closed.
setup.caption: 1. Sit 3 metres from the closed dabba. Fan off, windows shut.

setup.art: A parent lifting the lid of the dabba with one hand and starting a phone timer with the other.
setup.caption: 2. The lid comes off and the timer starts.

setup.art: The child raising a hand, eyes still closed, while the ceiling fan above turns.
setup.caption: 3. Raise your hand at the first smell. Then do it again with the fan on.

flow.do: 1. Close the windows and the door, and switch off the fan. 2. Put a stool at one end of the room, and a chair 3 metres away. 3. Outside the room, put the scented cotton in the dabba and close the lid. 4. Put the dabba on the stool and wait 2 minutes, so the air settles.
flow.say: We are going to time a smell. A smell is particles of a substance that have left it and mixed with the air.
flow.kid: Close the windows and door. Switch off the fan. Put a chair 3 metres from the stool. Sit on it and wait.
flow.context: This is the first step of Still Air or Fan. Here you set up a still room, with a closed box of scent 3 metres from your chair.

flow.do: 1. Ask for the guesses and the reasons. 2. Write them down.
flow.say: How many seconds will the smell take to reach you? Will the fan make it arrive sooner, later or never? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how many seconds the smell will take. Will the fan make it sooner or later? Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: The fan will blow the smell to me faster.
The fan will blow the smell away, so it will come later.
Smell particles move by themselves, so the fan will make no difference.

flow.context: This step of Still Air or Fan is for guessing how fast a smell crosses a room. You guess with and without a fan.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits on the chair, eyes closed, breathing normally. 2. Open the dabba and start the timer. 3. Stop the timer when your child raises a hand. If nothing is smelt in 5 minutes, write 'more than 300 seconds'. 4. Then your child walks slowly to the far corner, sniffs near the floor, and sniffs standing on tiptoe.
flow.say: Close your eyes and breathe normally. Raise your hand the moment you smell it. Then go and check the far corner, low down and high up.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Breathe normally. Raise your hand when you smell it. Then sniff in the far corner, low and high.
flow.parent: In a still room the smell often takes 1 to 4 minutes to cross 3 metres. Rooms differ a lot, though. Write down what really happens.
flow.context: This step of Still Air or Fan times the smell across 3 metres of still air. It also checks whether the smell reaches the far corner.

flow.do: 1. Close the dabba and take it out of the room. 2. Open the windows and switch the fan on for 5 minutes. 3. Your child waits in another room, so that the nose can rest. 4. Put a fresh scented cotton ball in the dabba, outside the room.
flow.say: Now we clear the room, so the second run starts fresh. A nose also gets used to a smell, so yours needs a rest.
flow.kid: Take the dabba out. Open the windows. Switch the fan on. Wait in another room for 5 minutes.
flow.context: This step of Still Air or Fan clears the old smell from the room. It also rests your nose before the second run.

flow.do: 1. Close the windows again and leave the fan on at its lowest speed. 2. Your child sits on the same chair, eyes closed. 3. Open the dabba on the stool and start the timer. 4. Stop it when your child raises a hand.
flow.say: Same chair, same smell, same distance. Only the fan is different. Raise your hand at the first smell.
flow.kid: Sit on the same chair. Close your eyes. The fan is on now. Raise your hand when you smell it.
flow.context: This step of Still Air or Fan times the same smell across the same 3 metres, with the fan on.

flow.do: 1. Look at the two times together. 2. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your two times. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The smell reached the far corner, low down and high up. What does that tell you about a gas?
good: It spreads out to fill the whole room.
It does not stay where it was let out.

flow.parent: With the fan on, the smell usually arrives within half a minute. Smell particles fly fast, but they hit air particles billions of times a second. So on their own they wander slowly. Moving air carries them along in bulk. Even with the fan off, a room has slow air currents. These did most of the carrying in the first run. Either way, the particles end up all through the room.

check.q: In Still Air or Fan, the smell reached the chair much sooner with the fan on. What carried it?
options: Moving air carried the smell particles along
The fan made new smell particles
The fan made the particles bigger
check.why: A fan moves air, and the smell particles mixed in that air travel with it. The fan makes no particles and does not change their size. In still air the particles spread too, but much more slowly.

flow.context: This is the last step of Still Air or Fan. Here you explain why the smell crossed the room faster with the fan on.

activities.title: Pour Air Upwards: catch a gas and move it
activities.context: This is the first thing to do in the lesson. You trap air in a tumbler under water, and then pour that air upwards into a second tumbler.

materials.item: a bucket or deep tub, three-quarters full of water
clear tumblers of the same size, glass or clear plastic
a towel

activities.record: Show where the air was before and after. Draw the two tumblers under water, or tell your grown-up.

setup.art: A hand pushing an upside-down clear tumbler straight down into a bucket of water, with the inside of the tumbler still full of air.
setup.caption: 1. Push tumbler A straight down, mouth first. The air stays inside.

setup.art: Under the water, tumbler A being tilted below tumbler B, which is upside down and full of water, with bubbles rising from A into B.
setup.caption: 2. Tilt A under B. The bubbles rise into B.

setup.art: Tumbler B now full of air and tumbler A full of water, both still under the surface.
setup.caption: 3. The air has moved from A to B.

flow.do: 1. Hold tumbler A upside down. 2. Push it straight down until it is under the water. 3. Look through its side.
flow.say: This tumbler looks empty. Push it under the water, mouth down. What do you see inside it?
flow.kid: Hold one tumbler upside down. Push it straight down into the water. Look through its side. Is it full of water?

ask.q: What is keeping the water out of the tumbler?
good: Air is inside it.
The air takes up the space, so the water has no room.

flow.context: This is the first step of Pour Air Upwards. Here you push an upside-down tumbler under water and see what stays inside it.

flow.do: 1. Lay tumbler B on its side under the water until it is full. 2. Turn it mouth down, still under the water. 3. Hold B just above A. 4. Tilt A slowly, so that the bubbles rise into B.
flow.say: Now pour the air from A up into B. Tilt A slowly. Where do the bubbles go? What happens to the water in B?
flow.kid: Fill tumbler B under the water. Turn it mouth down. Hold it above tumbler A. Tilt A slowly. Catch the bubbles in B.
flow.parent: Keep both mouths under the water all the time. If some bubbles miss, start again. It takes two or three tries to pour air neatly.
flow.context: This step of Pour Air Upwards moves the trapped air from one tumbler into another, under water.

flow.do: 1. Lift both tumblers out. 2. Ask your child what moved from A to B, and how they know it takes up space.
flow.say: You moved something from A to B. What was it? How do you know it takes up space?
flow.kid: Lift both tumblers out. Tell your grown-up what moved from A to B.
flow.think: You poured air upwards through water. Which way would you pour a gas that is heavier than air?

check.q: Air rose from one tumbler into another under water and pushed the water out. What does this show?
options: Air is a substance that takes up space
Water turns into air when a tumbler tilts
The first tumbler really was empty
check.why: The air could be caught, moved and used to push water out. So it is a real substance that takes up space. No water turned into air. The tumbler that looked empty was full of air all along.

flow.context: This is the last step of Pour Air Upwards. Here you say what moved from one tumbler to the other.

activities.title: Smoke in Two Jars: does a gas fill the space it is given?
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up fills one jar with agarbatti smoke and joins it to an empty jar. You watch where the smoke goes. The smoke shows what the air in the jar is doing.

materials.item: clear glass jars or glass tumblers with mouths of the same size
an agarbatti and a matchbox, for the grown-up
a stiff card, such as a postcard
a katori of water, to put the agarbatti out

activities.safety: A grown-up lights the agarbatti and puts it out in water afterwards. Do this near an open window, and do not breathe the smoke.
activities.record: Show where the smoke is at the start and after 3 minutes. Draw the two jars and shade the smoke, or take a photo of each.

setup.art: An upside-down glass jar held over a smoking agarbatti, filling with grey smoke.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up fills jar A with smoke and slides a card under it.

setup.art: The smoky jar standing mouth down on top of a clear jar, with a card between their mouths.
setup.caption: 2. Stand jar A on jar B, with the card between them.

setup.art: The same two jars with the card removed and thin grey smoke in both.
setup.caption: 3. Pull out the card. Watch for 3 minutes.
