flow.do: 1. Light the agarbatti. 2. Hold jar A upside down over the smoke for about 20 seconds, until it looks grey. 3. Slide the card under its mouth. 4. Put the agarbatti out in the water. 5. Stand jar A, still on its card, mouth to mouth on top of jar B.
flow.say: The smoke is in the top jar only. In a moment I will pull out the card. Where will the smoke go? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A grown-up fills the top jar with smoke. The card keeps it there.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: It will stay up, because smoke rises.
It will spread into both jars, because a gas spreads out.
It will all sink into the bottom jar.

flow.context: This is the first step of Smoke in Two Jars. Here a grown-up traps smoke in one jar, and you guess where it will go.

flow.do: 1. Hold both jars steady and pull the card out. 2. Watch for 3 minutes. 3. Compare how grey the top jar looks now with how it looked at the start.
flow.say: Watch both jars. What is the smoke doing? Is the top jar as grey as before?
flow.kid: The card is out. Watch both jars for 3 minutes. Where is the smoke now? Is the top jar as grey as before?
flow.parent: Within a few minutes there is smoke in both jars, and each looks thinner than the first jar did. Cool smoky air is a little heavier than clean air, so it drifts down as well as spreading.
flow.context: This step of Smoke in Two Jars lets the smoke into the second jar and watches where it goes.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they saw and why. 2. Then read them the note below.
flow.say: Say what you saw the smoke do. Why do you think it did that?
flow.kid: Tell your grown-up what the smoke did, and why.
flow.parent: Smoke is tiny solid and liquid bits floating in the air, and they go where the air goes. The gas in the top jar spread into all the space it was given. The same smoke in twice the space looks thinner.

check.q: Smoke filled one jar. Then a second jar was joined to it. What did the smoke do?
options: It stayed in the first jar only
It grew, so both jars looked just as grey
It spread through both jars and looked thinner
check.why: A gas spreads into all the space it can reach. No new smoke was made, so the same amount in twice the space looks thinner.

flow.context: This is the last step of Smoke in Two Jars. Here you say what the smoke did when it was given twice the space.

activities.title: How Much Gas Is One Breath?
activities.context: In this activity you blow one breath into an upturned bottle of water. The air pushes the water out, so you can measure the volume of your breath in millilitres.

materials.item: an empty two-litre plastic bottle with its cap
a 500 ml bottle or a measuring jug, and a marker pen
a bucket or tub half full of water
a clean flexible tube about 50 cm long, or two bendy straws joined with tape
a towel

activities.safety: Each person uses their own straw, or washes the end of the tube. Stop and rest if you feel dizzy after blowing hard.
activities.record: Write the volume of a quiet breath and of your deepest breath, in millilitres. Then work out the mass of each: one litre of air has a mass of about 1.2 grams.

setup.art: A two-litre bottle with marker lines on its side at 500, 1,000, 1,500 and 2,000 millilitres.
setup.caption: 1. Mark the bottle every 500 ml.

setup.art: The bottle full of water, held upside down with its mouth under the water in a bucket, and a tube leading up into its mouth.
setup.caption: 2. Turn the full bottle over in the bucket and push the tube into its mouth.

setup.art: A girl blowing into the tube, with a big bubble of air at the top of the upturned bottle and the water level pushed down.
setup.caption: 3. Blow one breath. The air pushes the water out.

flow.do: 1. Pour 500 ml of water into the two-litre bottle and mark the level. 2. Do this three more times, marking 1,000, 1,500 and 2,000 ml. 3. Add a short mark halfway between each pair of lines.
flow.say: First we turn this bottle into a measuring bottle. Each long line is 500 millilitres, and each short line is 250.
flow.kid: Pour in 500 ml of water. Mark the level. Do it three more times. Add short marks halfway between.
flow.context: This is the first step of How Much Gas Is One Breath? Here you mark a two-litre bottle so that it can measure volume.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess the volume of a quiet breath and of their deepest breath. 2. Ask for a reason. 3. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: How many millilitres of air do you breathe out in one quiet breath? And in your deepest breath? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how many millilitres are in one quiet breath. Guess for your deepest breath too. Say why.
flow.context: This step of How Much Gas Is One Breath? is for guessing the volume of your own breath.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bottle to the 2,000 ml line and cap it. 2. Turn it upside down, put its mouth under the water in the bucket, and take the cap off under water. 3. A grown-up holds the bottle. Push one end of the tube up into its mouth. 4. Breathe in quietly and breathe out quietly through the tube. 5. Cap the bottle under water, lift it out and stand it upright. 6. Read how much water is left, and take that away from 2,000.
flow.say: Breathe out one quiet breath through the tube. The air you breathe out takes the place of the water. How much water did it push out?
flow.kid: Turn the full bottle over in the bucket. Push the tube into its mouth. Breathe out quietly through the tube. Cap the bottle. Read the water left.
flow.parent: A quiet breath of a ten-year-old child is usually 250 to 400 ml. If 1,700 ml of water is left, the breath was 2,000 minus 1,700, which is 300 ml.
flow.context: This step of How Much Gas Is One Breath? measures one quiet breath by the water it pushes out of a bottle.

flow.do: 1. Refill the bottle and set it up again. 2. Your child takes the deepest breath they can and blows it all out through the tube. 3. Cap the bottle under water, lift it out and read the water left. 4. If you like, a grown-up tries too. 5. Work out the mass of each breath: about 1.2 grams for each litre.
flow.say: Now your deepest breath. Blow until no more comes out. How does it compare with the quiet breath?
flow.kid: Fill the bottle again. Take your deepest breath. Blow it all out through the tube. Read the water left. How big was this breath?
flow.parent: A ten-year-old child's deepest breath is often 1,500 to 2,500 ml. If the bottle empties, write 'more than 2,000 ml'. A grown-up's deepest breath is 3 to 5 litres, so it will empty the bottle. Some air always stays in the lungs, however hard you blow.

check.q: A deep breath pushed 1,500 ml of water out of an upturned bottle. What does that tell you?
options: The breath had a mass of 1,500 grams
The breath was about 1,500 ml of gas
The water turned into air
check.why: A gas takes up space, so the breath took the place of 1,500 ml of water. Its mass is tiny: about 1.2 grams a litre, so under 2 grams. The water did not change into anything. It was pushed out into the bucket.

flow.context: This is the last step of How Much Gas Is One Breath? Here you measure your deepest breath and compare it with a quiet one.

activities.title: 100 Grains of Air: build the mixture on a plate
activities.context: In this activity you build a model of air from kitchen grains. Each grain stands for one particle, so you can see how much of the air is each gas.

materials.item: raw rice
materials.qty: about a third of a cup

materials.item: moong dal, or any yellow dal
a black peppercorn and a clove
a steel plate and a teaspoon

activities.record: Lay your 100 grains in a square of 10 rows of 10. Keep the rice, the dal and the peppercorn each in their own part. Take a photo, or colour a paper square of 100 small squares the same way.

setup.art: A steel plate with a heap of 78 rice grains, a small heap of 21 yellow dal grains and one black peppercorn.
setup.caption: 1. Count 78 grains of rice, 21 of dal and 1 peppercorn.

setup.art: The same plate with the grains stirred together into one even mixture.
setup.caption: 2. Mix them. This is 100 particles of air.

setup.art: A larger heap of rice on the plate with one dark clove lying in it.
setup.caption: 3. One clove in a third of a cup of rice shows how rare carbon dioxide is.

flow.do: 1. Ask the question below before any counting. 2. Then count 78 grains of rice in tens. 3. Count 21 grains of dal. 4. Add one peppercorn.
flow.say: Air is a mixture of gases. Out of 100 particles of air, how many do you think are oxygen? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count 78 rice, 21 dal and 1 peppercorn into three small piles.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Most of it, because we need oxygen to breathe.
About half.
I think only a small part, because fires would burn too fast in pure oxygen.

flow.context: This is the first step of 100 Grains of Air. Here you guess how much of the air is oxygen, and then count out the grains.

flow.do: 1. Say that rice stands for nitrogen, dal for oxygen and the peppercorn for argon. 2. Stir the grains together with a finger. 3. Ask your child to point to where the oxygen is.
flow.say: The rice is nitrogen, the dal is oxygen, and the peppercorn is argon. Mix them well. Now, where on the plate is the oxygen?
flow.kid: Rice is nitrogen. Dal is oxygen. The peppercorn is argon. Mix them all with a finger. Then try to point to the oxygen.

ask.q: About what fraction of the air is oxygen?
good: About one-fifth.
21 out of 100.

flow.parent: The oxygen is everywhere on the plate, mixed evenly with the nitrogen. Real air is like this in every room and every country. Winds stir it, and gas particles spread among each other.
flow.context: This step of 100 Grains of Air mixes the grains. It shows that the gases in air are spread evenly among each other.

flow.do: 1. Say that carbon dioxide is only 4 particles in every 10,000. So one particle of it comes with about 2,500 others. 2. Count 100 grains of rice onto the teaspoon to see how much 100 is. 3. Pour a third of a cup of rice onto the plate. That is roughly 2,500 grains. 4. Drop in the clove.
flow.say: This heap is about 2,500 particles of air. The one clove is carbon dioxide. Plants build their whole bodies from a gas this rare.
flow.kid: Count 100 grains of rice onto a spoon. Now pour out a third of a cup. That is about 2,500 grains. Add one clove. The clove is carbon dioxide.

check.q: In 100 particles of dry air, about how many are nitrogen?
options: About 21
About 78
About 1
check.why: About 78 in 100 are nitrogen and about 21 are oxygen. Many people guess that air is mostly oxygen, because oxygen is the gas we need. Nitrogen goes in and out of our lungs unchanged.

flow.context: This is the last step of 100 Grains of Air. Here you see how rare carbon dioxide is in the air.

activities.title: Coins on the Floor: how far apart are the particles of a gas?
activities.context: In this activity coins stand for particles of water. You lay them out as a solid, as a liquid and as steam. Then you measure how much more space the steam needs.

materials.item: coins of the same kind, or bottle caps or carrom coins
a 30 cm ruler
a clear patch of floor, a little over 1 metre square
two long books or rulers, to act as walls

activities.record: Write the width of the block of coins as a liquid and as a gas. Work out how many times as wide the gas is.

setup.art: Sixteen coins on a tiled floor packed in a neat four-by-four square, touching each other, with a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Solid: 16 coins touching, in neat rows.

setup.art: The same sixteen coins touching but jumbled in a loose clump.
setup.caption: 2. Liquid: still touching, but jumbled.

setup.art: The sixteen coins spread in a wide four-by-four grid, each a ruler's length from the next, covering about a square metre of floor.
setup.caption: 3. Gas: each coin 12 coin-widths from the next.

flow.do: 1. Pack the 16 coins into a square of 4 rows of 4, all touching. This is ice. 2. Measure the width of the square. 3. Push the coins into a jumble, still touching. This is liquid water. 4. Measure the width again.
flow.say: These coins are particles of water. In ice they touch, in neat rows. In liquid water they still touch, but they slide about. How much space did each need?
flow.kid: Pack 16 coins in neat rows, all touching. That is ice. Now jumble them, still touching. That is water. Measure each block.
flow.context: This is the first step of Coins on the Floor. Here you lay out coins as the particles of a solid and of a liquid.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to show with their hands how far apart the particles will be in steam. 2. Ask for a reason. 3. Put two coins on the floor at the gap they guessed.
flow.say: When water boils into steam, how far apart do the particles go? Show me with two coins. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Water boils into steam. How far apart are the particles now? Show it with two coins. Say why.
flow.context: This step of Coins on the Floor is for guessing how far apart the particles of steam are.

flow.do: 1. Measure the width of one coin and multiply it by 12. For a coin 2.5 cm wide, that is 30 cm. 2. Lay the 16 coins in 4 rows of 4, with that gap between each coin and the next. 3. Measure the width of the whole square.
flow.say: In real steam, each particle is about 12 of its own widths from the next. Lay the coins out like that. How wide is the square now?
flow.kid: Measure one coin. Multiply by 12. Put the coins that far apart, in 4 rows of 4. Measure the whole square.

ask.q: What is in the gaps between the gas coins?
good: Nothing.
Empty space. It is not air, because the coins are the gas.

flow.parent: With coins 2.5 cm wide, the liquid block is about 10 cm wide. The gas square is about 1 metre wide. Real particles spread upwards as well as sideways. So steam takes about 12 times 12 times 12, or about 1,700, times the space of the water.
flow.context: This step of Coins on the Floor lays out the coins as the particles of steam. Each coin is 12 coin-widths from the next.

flow.do: 1. Put a long book on each side of the gas square, as walls. 2. Push the walls in until the gaps between the coins are halved. 3. Now try to push walls in on the liquid block.
flow.say: Push the walls in on the gas. Can the particles move closer? Now try the liquid. What is different?
flow.kid: Push the walls in on the gas coins. Then push them in on the liquid coins. Watch the gaps.
flow.parent: Cooking gas in a cylinder is squashed until its particles touch. At that point it has become a liquid.

check.q: A gas can be compressed into less space, but a liquid cannot. Why?
options: Gas particles are soft and liquid particles are hard
A liquid is heavier than a gas
Gas particles have gaps between them, and liquid particles touch
check.why: Compressing a gas pushes its particles into the empty space between them. In a liquid the particles already touch, so there is nowhere for them to go. The particles themselves do not get smaller or softer.

flow.context: This is the last step of Coins on the Floor. Here you squash the gas and the liquid, to see which can be compressed.

activities.title: Read the Cylinder: how is a gas sold by the kilogram?
activities.context: In this activity you and a grown-up read the numbers on the cooking gas cylinder at home. You work out how much the gas inside weighs, without touching the knob.

materials.item: the cooking gas cylinder at home, to look at only
a torch, a pencil and paper
the last gas bill or booking message, if you have one
if your home has piped gas or no gas: a deodorant can, to read its label

activities.safety: A grown-up stays with the child. Look only. Do not move the cylinder or touch the knob or the pipe.
activities.record: Write the empty mass painted on the cylinder, add 14.2 kg, and write the mass of the full cylinder.

setup.art: A child and her mother crouching by a red gas cylinder under a kitchen counter, shining a torch at the inside of its top ring.
setup.caption: 1. With a grown-up, find the number painted inside the top ring.

setup.art: A notebook page with the sum 15.3 kg plus 14.2 kg written on it.
setup.caption: 2. Add 14.2 kg of gas to the empty mass.

flow.do: 1. Go to the cylinder together. 2. Shine the torch on the inside of the ring at the top. 3. Find a painted number between 14 and 18, such as 15.3. 4. Write it down.
flow.say: Every cylinder has a number painted inside its top ring. It is the mass of the empty steel cylinder, in kilograms. What does ours say?
flow.kid: Go to the gas cylinder with a grown-up. Look only. Find the number painted inside the top ring. Write it down.
flow.parent: The number is called the tare weight. If your home has no cylinder, read a deodorant can instead. Its label gives the mass of what is inside in grams, and says it is under pressure.
flow.context: This is the first step of Read the Cylinder. Here you find the mass of the empty cylinder, which is painted on it.

flow.do: 1. Say that a full home cylinder holds 14.2 kg of gas. The bill usually says so. 2. Ask your child to add the two numbers. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: A full cylinder holds 14.2 kilograms of gas. Add that to the painted number. What do you get?
flow.kid: A full cylinder holds 14.2 kg of gas. Add it to the painted number.

ask.q: How can so much gas fit in one cylinder?
good: It is squeezed very hard.
It is squeezed until it turns into a liquid.

flow.context: This step of Read the Cylinder works out the mass of a full cylinder. It also asks how so much gas fits inside.

flow.do: 1. Say that as a gas in the room, 14.2 kg of cooking gas would fill about 7,000 litres. 2. Ask how many 20-litre buckets that is. 3. Ask how the gas company could check how much gas is left in a cylinder.
flow.say: Let out as a gas, it would fill about 7,000 litres. How many 20-litre buckets is that? And how could we tell how much gas is left?
flow.kid: As a gas, it would fill 7,000 litres. How many 20-litre buckets is that? How could you tell how much gas is left?
flow.parent: 7,000 divided by 20 is 350 buckets. To find the gas left, weigh the cylinder and take away the painted number.

check.q: How does 14.2 kg of cooking gas fit into one home cylinder?
options: It is compressed until it becomes a liquid
The cylinder is far bigger inside than outside
A gas takes up no space at all
check.why: A gas has empty space between its particles, so it can be compressed. Cooking gas is compressed until the particles touch and it becomes a liquid, which takes far less space.

flow.context: This is the last step of Read the Cylinder. Here you compare the gas squeezed in the cylinder with the space it would fill in a room.

activities.title: The Compare Table: a solid, a liquid and a gas, tested side by side
activities.context: In this activity you give a solid, a liquid and a gas the same four tests. Then you fill in a table that compares the three states.

materials.item: plastic bottles of the same size, about 500 ml, with caps
water, to fill one bottle to the brim
dry sand, rava or sugar, to fill one bottle to the brim
a steel spoon and a bowl

activities.record: Draw a table with three rows: solid, liquid, gas. Give it four columns: keeps its shape, keeps its volume, flows, can be squashed. Fill it with yes or no.

setup.art: Three capped plastic bottles in a row: one full of water, one full of sand and one holding only air.
setup.caption: 1. Fill one bottle with water, one with sand, and leave one with air. Cap all three.

setup.art: A child's hands squeezing the air bottle, whose sides bend inwards.
setup.caption: 2. Squeeze each capped bottle hard.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of three rows and four columns, half filled with yes and no.
setup.caption: 3. Fill in the table.

flow.do: 1. Fill one bottle to the very brim with water and cap it. 2. Fill one to the brim with sand, rava or sugar and cap it. 3. Cap the third with only air in it. 4. Ask which bottles will squeeze in, and why. 5. Squeeze each one hard.
flow.say: Three bottles: water, sand and air. Which will squeeze in when you press it? Why do you think so? Now try.
flow.kid: Fill one bottle with water and one with sand. Leave one with air. Cap all three. Squeeze each one hard.
flow.parent: The air bottle squeezes in. The water bottle hardly moves if no air bubble is left under the cap. The sand bottle hardly moves either.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Compare Table. Here you squeeze a bottle of liquid, a bottle of solid grains and a bottle of gas.

flow.do: 1. Put the steel spoon in the bowl, then pour a little water in beside it. 2. Ask which keeps its shape and which takes the bowl's shape. 3. Uncap the air bottle and ask where its air can go now. 4. Fill in the table together.
flow.say: The spoon, the water and the air: which keeps its own shape? Which keeps its own volume? Which flows?
flow.kid: Put the spoon in the bowl. Pour in some water. Fill in your table.

ask.q: Which property do water and air share, that the spoon does not have?
good: They flow.
They take the shape of their container.

ask.q: Which property does only the air have?
good: It can be squashed.
It has no volume of its own, so it spreads out.

flow.context: This step of The Compare Table fills in the table for a steel spoon, water and air.

flow.do: 1. Pour the sand into the bowl. 2. Ask whether sand is a solid or a liquid, and why. 3. Look closely at a few grains together.
flow.say: Sand pours and takes the shape of the bowl. So is sand a liquid? Look at one grain before you answer.
flow.kid: Pour the sand into the bowl. It flows like water. Look closely at one grain.
flow.parent: Each grain keeps its own shape, so each grain is a solid. A heap pours because the grains roll over each other, with air in the gaps.

check.q: Which property belongs to a gas, but not to a solid or a liquid?
options: It spreads to fill all the space it gets
It has mass
It is made of particles
check.why: Only a gas has no volume of its own, so only a gas spreads to fill its container. All three states have mass, and all three are made of particles.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Compare Table. Here you decide whether sand, which pours, is a solid or a liquid.

projects.title: Five Sticky Squares: where is the air around our home dustiest?
projects.context: In this four-day project you put five greased squares in five places in and around your home. After three days you count the specks each one has caught, to compare the dust floating in the air.

materials.item: pieces of clear stiff plastic or white card, about 6 cm by 8 cm (cut from a food box lid or an old folder)
petroleum jelly
materials.qty: a small dab for each piece

materials.item: a marker pen, a ruler and sticky tape
a magnifying glass, or a phone camera to zoom in
a sheet of white paper
a weather app that shows the Air Quality Index

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the plastic. Tape the square near the stove at least an arm's length from the flame.

schedule.what: Make five sticky squares and tape them up in five places. Guess which will catch the most specks, and say why. Write down today's AQI.
Write down today's AQI. Check that all five squares are still in place.
Write down today's AQI. Look at the squares without touching them.
Collect the squares, count the specks on each, draw a bar chart and write what you found.

projects.record: Make a table: place, my guess of its rank, number of specks. Make a bar chart with one bar for each place, drawn or made of bottle caps. Then write what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

setup.art: A piece of clear plastic with a rectangle 4 cm long and 2 cm wide drawn on it, divided into eight small squares, and a finger smearing jelly over it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a 4 cm by 2 cm rectangle on each piece, and grease it thinly.

setup.art: A greased square taped upright to a balcony grille that faces a busy road.
setup.caption: 2. Tape the squares up in five places for three days.

setup.art: Five squares laid on white paper, with a phone camera zoomed in on dark specks stuck inside one rectangle.
setup.caption: 3. Count the specks inside each rectangle.

flow.do: 1. On each piece, draw a rectangle 4 cm long and 2 cm wide. Divide it into 8 squares of 1 cm. Label the pieces A to E. 2. Smear a thin layer of petroleum jelly over each rectangle. 3. Tape the pieces upright in five places. Put one near the stove and one on a bedroom shelf. Put one at a window facing the road, one by the front door and one at a quiet window. 4. Ask your child to rank the five places from most specks to fewest, with reasons. 5. Write down today's AQI from the weather app.
flow.say: Air carries tiny solid bits that we mostly cannot see. Which of these five places will catch the most in three days? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw a rectangle on each piece. Grease it thinly. Tape the pieces up in five places. Rank the places, most specks first.
flow.parent: Keep every square upright and out of the rain, so that the test is fair. Upright squares catch what floats past in the air, more than what falls from above.
flow.context: This is the first step of Five Sticky Squares. Here you make five greased squares, put them in five places and guess which will catch the most dust.

flow.do: 1. On days 2 and 3, write down the AQI. 2. Look at each square without touching it. 3. Leave the squares where they are.
flow.say: What is the AQI today? Can you see anything on the squares yet?
flow.kid: Write today's AQI. Look at each square. Do not touch them.
flow.context: This step of Five Sticky Squares is the daily check. You record the Air Quality Index and leave the squares in place.

flow.do: 1. On day 4, collect the squares and lay them on white paper. 2. Count the dark specks inside each rectangle, with the magnifying glass or the phone camera. If there are too many, count 2 small squares and multiply by 4. 3. Make a bar chart. Draw it, or line up bottle caps, one cap for every 10 specks. 4. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: Count the specks in each rectangle. Then say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Collect the squares. Count the specks in each rectangle. Make your bar chart.

ask.q: Where did the specks at the busiest place come from?
good: Smoke and dust from traffic.
Soot and oil droplets from cooking, for the square near the stove.

ask.q: A square looks clean. Does that prove the air there was clean?
good: No. The smallest bits and the harmful gases are too small to see.
It shows only that few big specks floated past.

flow.parent: The square by the road or the stove usually catches the most. The squares show only specks big enough to see. PM2.5 and polluting gases do not show, so use the AQI numbers as well.

check.q: One sticky square caught far more specks than the other four. What is the fairest thing to say?
options: The other four places have perfectly clean air
That place has no air fit to breathe
More dust floated in the air at that place
check.why: The count compares the dust that floated past each square. It does not show that the other places are clean. The smallest bits and the gases do not show on a sticky square.

flow.context: This is the last step of Five Sticky Squares. Here you count the specks on each square and compare the five places.

challenges.title: A Mask That Stops Dust and Still Lets You Breathe
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about air pollution. Air is a gas with tiny solid bits floating in it. You design a cloth mask that catches the bits but lets the gas through.
challenges.problem: Design the best filter you can from cloth and paper at home. It must stop as much powder as possible in the puff test. It must also let enough air through for a person to breathe.
constraints: Use only cloth, tissue paper and rubber bands from home.
The filter must cover the whole mouth of the test bowl.
Give each design the same test: 3 puffs of powder from 5 cm above the cloth.
Each design must also pass the breath test: when you blow through it, a tissue strip 15 cm away must still move.
materials: a dry squeezy bottle, such as an empty ketchup or dish-wash bottle
half a teaspoon of talcum powder or fine rice flour
a steel bowl about 12 cm across, with a piece of dark paper or dark cloth in the bottom
a cotton handkerchief, a dupatta or other thin cloth, an old banian and tissue paper
a strip of tissue paper about 2 cm wide and 15 cm long
challenges.safety: Do the puff test beside an open window or on a balcony. Keep faces away from the puff, and do not breathe the powder.
general: Two layers of a cotton handkerchief.
A thin dupatta folded into four layers.
A shop-bought surgical mask laid flat over the bowl.
creative: A layer of tissue paper between two layers of cloth.
Cloth with small folds in it, so that more cloth covers the same opening.
A slightly damp cloth, to see whether wet threads catch more powder.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own filter. Plan it by drawing it or by telling your grown-up the layers. Then build it and give it both tests. Which design stopped the most powder and still passed the breath test?

setup.art: A steel bowl with dark paper in the bottom and a white handkerchief stretched over its mouth, held by a rubber band.
setup.caption: 1. Stretch the cloth over a bowl with dark paper inside.

setup.art: A hand squeezing a plastic bottle so that a small puff of white powder hits the cloth from just above.
setup.caption: 2. Puff powder at the cloth 3 times from 5 cm above.

setup.art: The cloth lifted off to show a light dusting of white powder on the dark paper in the bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Lift the cloth. How much powder got through?

setup.art: A child blowing through a folded cloth at a strip of tissue paper held up by a parent.
setup.caption: 4. Blow through the same cloth. Does the tissue strip still move?

flow.do: 1. Put the powder in the squeezy bottle. 2. Lay the dark paper in the bowl. Puff 3 times from 5 cm above the open bowl. Look at the paper, then wipe it clean. 3. Stretch one layer of thin cloth over the bowl with a rubber band. Puff 3 times again. 4. Lift the cloth and compare the paper with the first try.
flow.say: First we see what three puffs leave on the paper with no filter at all. Then we try one thin layer of cloth. How much powder got through?
flow.kid: Puff powder into the open bowl 3 times. Look at the paper. Wipe it. Cover the bowl with one cloth. Puff again. How much got through?
flow.parent: Give each result a score: 2 for a lot of powder on the paper, 1 for a little, 0 for none you can see.
flow.context: This is the first step of the mask challenge. Here you test three puffs of powder with no filter, and then with one layer of cloth.

flow.do: 1. Choose one of the usual designs. 2. Give it the puff test and write its score. 3. Give it the breath test: hold it over your mouth and blow at the tissue strip from 15 cm. 4. Test a second design in the same way.
flow.say: More layers stop more powder. But can you still breathe through them? Test both things each time.
flow.kid: Pick a design. Puff 3 times. Write the score. Then blow through it at the tissue strip. Does the strip move?
flow.context: This step of the mask challenge tests two usual designs. You find how much powder each stops and how easily air passes.

flow.do: 1. Build your own design. 2. Give it both tests. 3. Compare all the scores and pick the best.
flow.say: Which design is best? What did you have to give up to stop more powder?
flow.kid: Build your own design. Test it both ways. Write down each score.
flow.parent: No cloth mask stops the very smallest bits, the PM2.5. Masks sold as N95 use a mat of very fine fibres to catch most of them.

check.q: A cloth mask lets air through but stops much of the dust. Why?
options: The cloth makes new clean air
Air is lighter than dust and floats past
Dust bits are much bigger than gas particles
check.why: Gas particles are far smaller than the gaps between threads, so they pass through. A bit of dust is many thousands of times bigger and gets caught on the threads. The cloth makes no air. It only sorts the gas from the solid bits.

flow.context: This is the last step of the mask challenge. Here you test your own design and choose the best filter.

challenges.title: Catch the Gas and Measure It
challenges.context: This is a measuring challenge. In Two Balloons on a Hanger, the gas from the fizz filled a balloon. But nobody knew how many millilitres there were. Here you find a way to measure it.
challenges.problem: Catch the gas made by 1 level teaspoon of baking soda and 50 ml of vinegar. Measure its volume in millilitres.
constraints: Catch as much of the gas as you can. Gas that leaks is gas you cannot measure.
Do it twice, to see whether you get nearly the same answer.
materials: a small plastic bottle of 250 to 500 ml with its cap
a two-litre bottle marked every 250 ml
a bucket half full of water
a flexible tube about 50 cm long
atta dough or modelling clay, to seal the tube into the cap
100 ml of vinegar, 2 level teaspoons of baking soda and some tissue paper
challenges.safety: A grown-up makes the hole in the bottle cap. Keep faces away from the bottle mouth.
general: Fit a balloon over the bottle, as in Two Balloons on a Hanger, and measure round the balloon. This gives a size, but not millilitres.
Fix a thin plastic bag, squashed flat, over the bottle mouth with a rubber band. Then push the full bag under water in a brim-full bowl and measure the water that spills.
Lead a tube from the bottle cap into an upturned bottle full of water. The gas pushes the water out, and the marks show the volume.
creative: Weigh the bottle before and after the fizz, as in Weigh the Fizz. Divide the grams lost by 1.8. A litre of carbon dioxide has a mass of about 1.8 grams.
Wrap the baking soda in tissue, so that the fizz starts only after the cap is on.
Use twice as much of both, and see whether you catch twice as much gas.
challenges.your_turn: Now choose your method, or invent one. Measure the gas twice. How close were your two answers? Where could gas have escaped?

setup.art: A small plastic bottle with a tube sealed into a hole in its cap with a ring of dough.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes a hole in the cap and seals the tube into it.

setup.art: A marked two-litre bottle full of water, upside down in a bucket, with the tube from the small bottle leading up into its mouth.
setup.caption: 2. Lead the tube into an upturned bottle of water.

setup.art: The small bottle fizzing, bubbles rising inside the upturned bottle and the water level pushed down to a mark.
setup.caption: 3. The gas pushes the water out. Read the marks.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem and the three usual methods together. 2. Ask your child to choose a method and say why. 3. For the tube method, a grown-up makes a hole in the cap and pushes the tube through. Then they seal round it with dough.
flow.say: We need to catch a gas and measure its volume. Which method do you want to try? What could go wrong with it?
flow.kid: Read the problem. Look at the three methods. Choose one. Say why you chose it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Catch the Gas and Measure It. Here you choose a way to catch and measure the gas.

flow.do: 1. Fill the marked bottle to the 2,000 ml line and cap it. Turn it over in the bucket, and take the cap off under water. 2. Push the free end of the tube up into its mouth. 3. Pour 50 ml of vinegar into the small bottle. 4. Wrap 1 level teaspoon of baking soda in tissue and drop it in. Screw the cap with the tube on at once. 5. Swirl until the bubbling stops. 6. Cap the big bottle under water, stand it upright and read the water left. Take that away from 2,000.
flow.say: Watch the bubbles rise into the big bottle. Each bubble is gas taking the place of water. How many millilitres did we catch?
flow.kid: Set up the big bottle upside down in the bucket. Start the fizz in the small bottle. Cap it fast. Watch the bubbles. Read the marks.
flow.parent: Expect somewhere between 600 and 1,100 ml. Some gas stays dissolved in the vinegar, and some escapes before the cap is on. The first bubbles are air pushed out of the small bottle. That is fine, because the gas has taken its place.
flow.context: This step of Catch the Gas and Measure It runs the tube method and reads the volume of gas caught.

flow.do: 1. Do it a second time and compare the two answers. 2. Then change one thing to make the method better, or try twice the amounts. 3. Ask where gas could have escaped.
flow.say: How close were your two answers? What would you change to lose less gas?
flow.kid: Do it again. Are the two answers close? Change one thing to make it better.

check.q: Gas from a fizz pushed 900 ml of water out of an upturned bottle. What is the volume of the gas caught?
options: About 900 grams
Nothing, because a gas takes up no space
About 900 ml
check.why: The gas took the place of the water, so its volume is the volume of water pushed out. Millilitres measure space, and grams measure mass. 900 ml of carbon dioxide has a mass of under 2 grams.

flow.context: This is the last step of Catch the Gas and Measure It. Here you repeat the measurement and improve your method.

items.p: Which of these is a gas at room temperature?
items.why: Oxygen is a gas: it has no shape or volume of its own. Coconut oil and honey are liquids, and salt is a solid.

items.p: True or false: a tumbler with nothing poured into it is empty.
items.why: False. The tumbler is full of air, which is a mixture of gases. A strong answer gives evidence, such as an upturned tumbler keeping water out.

items.p: A gas spreads out to fill all the space in its ____.
items.why: A gas has no volume of its own. Its particles fly freely until walls stop them, so it fills whatever holds it.

items.p: Sort these into solid, liquid or gas.
items.why: Solids keep their shape. Liquids flow but keep their volume. Gases spread to fill their container. A strong answer can give the property used for each.

items.p: At room temperature, carbon dioxide, hydrogen and water vapour are all ____.
items.why: All three are gases at room temperature, in a normal warm room. Water vapour is water as a gas.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could give a home example of each.
pairs: to squash into a smaller space
the layer of air around the Earth
how much matter a thing is made of
how much space a thing takes up

items.p: Two balloons are the same size. The carbon dioxide balloon sinks lower on a balance than the air balloon. Explain why.
items.a: Both balloons held the same volume of gas. Carbon dioxide particles are heavier than the particles of air. So the same volume of carbon dioxide has more mass, and its end of the hanger went down.
items.why: A strong answer says that the sizes were the same, so the difference must come from the gas. It also says that both gases have mass.

items.p: Baking soda is added to vinegar, and the mix fizzes. What state is the new substance in the bubbles?
items.why: The bubbles are carbon dioxide, a gas made when the solid and the liquid meet. Choosing 'no new substance' treats the fizz as air that was hiding in the vinegar.

items.p: Draw the particles of a solid, a liquid and a gas in three boxes of the same size.
items.a: Solid: many particles touching, in neat rows. Liquid: about as many particles, touching but jumbled. Gas: only one or two particles, far apart, with arrows to show them flying.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps the particles the same size in all three boxes, and leaves the gas box almost empty.
items.art: Three empty boxes in a row, labelled solid, liquid and gas.

items.p: Three of these are gases in the air. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Nitrogen, oxygen and argon are the three main gases of dry air. Salt is a solid.

items.p: True or false: a gas has mass.
items.why: True. A fizzing mix gets lighter as its gas leaves, and a ball gets heavier when air is pumped in. A litre of air has a mass of about 1.2 grams.

items.p: These are the steps for making a gas and catching it in a balloon. Put them in order.
a: Put baking soda into a flat balloon
Fit the balloon over the bottle mouth
Tip the baking soda into the vinegar
Tie the balloon when the fizzing stops
items.why: The solid and the liquid must meet only after the balloon is fitted. Otherwise the gas escapes before it can be caught.
items: Tip the baking soda into the vinegar
Tie the balloon when the fizzing stops
Fit the balloon over the bottle mouth
Put baking soda into a flat balloon

items.p: Label a drawing of an upside-down tumbler pushed under water: trapped air, water inside the tumbler, water outside.
a: Trapped air at the top of the tumbler
Water inside the tumbler, only a little way up
items.why: The air takes up space, so the water can rise only a little way inside the tumbler.
items.art: An upside-down tumbler under water in a bucket, with blank label lines.

items.p: Two children look at a bottle with nothing poured into it. They disagree about it.
items.a: A strong answer agrees that the bottle is full of air. It gives evidence from a test, such as trapped air keeping water out. It also sees that the first child uses 'empty' the everyday way. To that child, it means that nothing we put there is inside.
items.why: In science the second child is right. But the everyday word 'empty' is useful too, and the two meanings need not fight.

views.says: The bottle is empty. I can see right through it, and nothing pours out.
The bottle is full. Air is a substance, even though I cannot see it.

items.ask: Which child do you agree with? Give evidence from a test. Then say what the other child means by 'empty'.

items.p: About how much of the air is nitrogen?
items.why: About 78 in 100 are nitrogen, 21 are oxygen and 1 is argon. Choosing 21 mixes nitrogen up with oxygen.

items.p: Name two things in your home that hold a gas. Say what each gas is used for.
items.a: For example: a cooking gas cylinder holds LPG, which burns to cook food. A cycle tyre holds compressed air, which makes the ride soft. A packet of chips holds nitrogen, which keeps the chips crisp.
items.why: A strong answer names a real container, the gas inside it and what the gas does.

worksheets.title: Why Gases Behave As They Do (stretch)

items.p: Why does a gas spread out to fill a whole room?
opts: The walls pull the gas towards them
Its particles fly freely in all directions
Air pushes it into the corners
items.why: Gas particles are not held together. Each flies until it hits something, so in time they are spread through all the space. The particles do not grow, and nothing pulls or pushes them into place.

items.p: A capped bottle of air squeezes in. A capped bottle full of water does not. Explain why, using particles.
items.a: In air the particles are far apart, with empty space between them, so squeezing pushes them closer. In water the particles already touch, so they have nowhere to go.
items.why: A strong answer talks about the empty space between gas particles, not about the particles being soft or small.

items.p: True or false: the space between the particles of a gas is filled with air.
items.why: False. Between the particles there is empty space. Air is itself made of particles, so there is no 'air' left over to fill the gaps.

items.p: Cooking gas is compressed in its cylinder until it becomes a ____.
items.why: Compressing pushes the particles together until they touch. Then the gas has become a liquid, which takes far less space.

items.p: Sort these gases: is each one lighter than air, or heavier than air?
items.why: Helium, hydrogen and natural gas have light particles, so they rise in air. Carbon dioxide and cooking gas have heavy particles, so they sink.

items.p: A box holds 36 particles of liquid water. Draw the same box holding steam. How many particles belong in it?
items.a: At most one particle, and often none. In steam each particle is about 12 widths from the next. So a box 6 particles wide has room for less than one.
items.why: A strong drawing is almost empty. Most drawings of gases show far too many particles.
items.art: Two boxes of the same size, the first filled with 36 touching dots and the second left blank.

items.p: A family wants a gas-leak alarm in the kitchen. Two fitters give opposite advice.
items.a: A strong answer says both can be right, because it depends on the gas. Cooking gas from a cylinder is heavier than air and collects low down. Piped natural gas is lighter than air and collects high up. So the family must first find out which gas they use.
items.why: Different gases have different densities, so no single rule fits every gas.

views.says: Fit the alarm near the floor. Leaked gas is heavy and sinks.
Fit the alarm near the ceiling. Leaked gas is light and rises.

items.ask: Which fitter would you trust? Say what you would need to know about the home first, and why.

items.p: A balloon of air hangs from a balance in a room. Why does the air inside add almost nothing?
opts: The rubber is too thin to hold mass
The air inside has leaked out
The air around the balloon holds it up
items.why: The air inside has mass, but the air outside pushes the balloon up by nearly the same amount. Choosing 'air has no mass' forgets that a pumped ball gets heavier.

items.p: Put these in order, from particles closest together to particles farthest apart.
a: Air pumped into a cycle tyre
Air at the top of Mount Everest
items.why: Liquid particles touch. Tyre air is compressed, so its particles are closer than in room air. High on a mountain the air is thin, so its particles are farthest apart.
items: Air at the top of Mount Everest
Air pumped into a cycle tyre

items.p: Match each gas to a place where you meet it.
items.why: Each gas is chosen for what it does: nitrogen does not spoil food, helium is light, and oxygen keeps us alive.
pairs: a cylinder beside a hospital bed
the red cylinder in a kitchen

items.p: Three of these are two states mixed together. Which one is a single state?
items.why: Fog is liquid drops in a gas, and smoke is solid bits in a gas. Foam is gas bubbles in a liquid. Nitrogen is only a gas.

items.p: A smell crosses a room faster when the fan is on. What does that tell you about how smells travel?
items.a: Smell particles are mixed into the air, so when the air moves, they move with it. On their own they spread slowly, because they keep bumping into air particles. The fan carries them along quickly.
items.why: A strong answer separates two things: particles spreading by themselves, and moving air carrying them.

items.p: Label a bottle with a balloon on top: vinegar, baking soda, carbon dioxide. Write the state beside each.
a: Baking soda: solid, falling in from the balloon
Carbon dioxide: gas, filling the balloon
items.why: A liquid and a solid meet and make a new substance, which is a gas.
items.art: A plastic bottle with liquid in the bottom and a part-filled balloon on its mouth, with blank label lines.

items.p: True or false: the white cloud above a boiling kettle is water as a gas.
items.why: False. Water as a gas is invisible. The white cloud is tiny drops of liquid water, formed where the hot vapour cools in the air.

items.p: A deep breath pushes 1,800 ml of water out of a bottle. About what is the mass of that air?
items.why: A litre of air has a mass of about 1.2 grams. 1.8 litres times 1.2 is about 2.2 grams. Choosing 1,800 grams mixes up millilitres of air with grams of water.

items.p: In 1894, nitrogen taken from air weighed slightly more than nitrogen made from chemicals. Two scientists disagree about it.
items.a: A strong answer sees that a small difference which comes back every time is evidence, not a slip. It suggests a test, such as removing everything known from air and seeing whether any gas is left. Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay did this and found argon.
items.why: Both views are reasonable at first. Repeating the measurement is what separates a mistake from a discovery.

views.says: The difference is only 1 part in 200. It is surely a small mistake in the weighing.
The same difference comes back every time. Something heavier must be hiding in the air.

items.ask: Would you ignore the difference or chase it? Say why, and describe one test that could settle it.

items.p: A closed bottle of fizzing vinegar and soda keeps its mass. Opened, it loses 3 grams. Explain both results.
items.a: The fizz makes carbon dioxide gas, which has mass. While the bottle is closed, the gas stays inside, so the mass stays the same. When the cap opens, gas rushes out, and its mass leaves with it.
items.why: A strong answer uses one idea, that a gas has mass, to explain both results.

items.p: One litre of carbon dioxide is 0.6 g heavier than one litre of air. How much heavier are 2 litres?
items.why: Twice the volume holds twice the extra mass. 0.6 times 2 is 1.2 grams.

items.p: True or false: cooking gas that leaks from a cylinder collects near the ceiling.
items.why: False. Cooking gas from a cylinder is heavier than air, so it sinks and collects near the floor. That is why people open the doors and windows and do not touch any switch.

items.p: The upward push of the air on a balloon is called ____.
items.why: Upthrust is the upward push of a gas or a liquid on anything inside it. It equals the weight of the gas or liquid pushed aside.

items.p: Draw the Earth with its layer of air. Show where the air is thickest and how it changes higher up.
items.a: A thin layer round the Earth, shaded darkest at the ground and fading upwards, with no sharp top line.
items.why: A strong drawing makes the layer very thin compared with the Earth, and lets it fade out without an edge.
items.art: A circle for the Earth with blank space around it.

items.p: Sort these: is it only a gas, or tiny solids and liquids floating in a gas?
items.why: Oxygen, nitrogen, water vapour and carbon dioxide are gases, and all are invisible. Smoke, fog, haze and spray can be seen because they hold tiny solid or liquid bits.

items.p: A sticky square by the road catches 40 specks. One in a bedroom catches 5. What is the fairest conclusion?
opts: The bedroom air has no dust at all
Road air holds 40 kinds of gas
More dust floats in air by the road
The bedroom square was not sticky
items.why: The squares compare the dust that floats past. Five specks is still some dust, and the smallest bits do not show at all.

items.p: A litre of each is weighed. Put them in order, from the smallest mass to the largest.
items.why: Hydrogen has the lightest particles, then helium. Air is heavier, and carbon dioxide heavier still. Water is a liquid, with its particles touching, so a litre of it has a mass of a whole kilogram.

items.p: A friend says, 'Gases always rise.' Describe one test or example that shows this is not always true.
items.a: For example: a balloon filled with carbon dioxide falls faster than a balloon of air, and sinks on a balance. Leaked cooking gas collects near the floor. A gas rises only if it is lighter than the air around it.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real case and then states the rule that replaces 'always'.

items.p: Match each idea about gases to the evidence for it.
items.why: Each idea in science stands on evidence. A strong answer could describe a second piece of evidence for one of them.
pairs: trapped air keeps water out of an upturned tumbler
an open tumbler of fizz gets lighter
smoke spreads from one jar into two
a capped bottle of air squeezes in
a balloon of carbon dioxide sinks below a balloon of air

items.p: Label a pie chart of dry air with three slices: nitrogen, oxygen, and argon with other gases.
a: Thin sliver: argon and other gases, about 1 in 100
items.why: Nitrogen is nearly four-fifths of the air and oxygen about one-fifth.
items.art: A circle divided into one large slice, one smaller slice and one thin sliver, with blank label lines.

items.p: Why is the mix of gases in air almost the same in Chennai and in Shimla?
opts: Each city makes its own air
The heavy gases all stay in Chennai
Winds stir the air, and gases mix
items.why: Gases spread to fill the space they reach, and winds mix the whole atmosphere. Shimla has less air in each breath than Chennai, but the same mix.

items.p: Three of these lower air pollution. Which one adds to it?
opts: Burning dry leaves in a heap
Cooking on gas, not smoky wood
items.why: Burning leaves puts smoke straight into the air. Shared buses, covered building sites and cleaner cooking fuel all put less smoke and dust into it.

items.p: Glass keeps its shape, but its particles are jumbled like a liquid's. Is glass a solid? Give your reasons.
items.a: For example: glass is a solid, because it keeps its own shape and volume and does not flow. But it is an unusual solid, because its particles are not in neat rows. This shows that the three states are useful boxes, and some things sit near the edge of a box.
items.why: A strong answer uses the properties of states to decide, and admits that the fit is not perfect.

quiz.p: A tumbler is pushed mouth-down into water, and the inside stays mostly dry. Why?
opts: The water is too heavy to rise
The air inside takes up the space
quiz.why: Air is a substance that takes up space, so the water has no room to rise. The glass and the size of the tumbler make no difference.

quiz.p: Which test best shows that a gas has mass?
opts: A fizzing mix gets lighter as gas leaves
quiz.why: If mass leaves the scale when only gas leaves, the gas must have mass. Wind shows that air can push, but not that it has mass.

quiz.p: Perfume is opened in one corner of a closed room. An hour later, where is the smell?
quiz.why: The particles of a gas keep moving until they are spread through all the space they can reach.

quiz.p: In which state are the particles far apart and flying freely in all directions?
quiz.why: In a solid and a liquid the particles touch. Only in a gas are they far apart and free.

quiz.p: Which property do liquids and gases share, but solids do not have?
opts: They flow and take their container's shape
quiz.why: Liquids and gases both flow. Only gases can be squashed easily, and all three states have mass.

quiz.p: A litre of milk is poured from a jug into a wide pan. What stays the same?
quiz.why: A liquid takes the shape of its container but keeps its volume. A litre is still a litre in any vessel.

quiz.p: Which gas makes up about one-fifth of the air, and is the gas our bodies use?
quiz.why: About 21 in every 100 particles of air are oxygen. Nitrogen is nearly four-fifths, but our bodies breathe it in and out unchanged.

quiz.p: Water is in the air on a humid day, but you cannot see it. What state is this water in?
opts: A liquid, in tiny drops you can see
quiz.why: Water vapour is water as a gas, and it is invisible. The tiny drops you can see in fog or a cloud are liquid water, not vapour. Frost is solid water.

quiz.p: Vinegar is a liquid and baking soda is a solid. They fizz together. What is made?
quiz.why: The fizz is bubbles of carbon dioxide, a new substance in a third state. Choosing 'nothing new' treats the bubbles as air that was already there.

quiz.p: Two balloons are the same size. One holds carbon dioxide and one holds air. Why is the first heavier?
opts: Its particles are heavier, and just as many
quiz.why: The same space holds about the same number of gas particles. Carbon dioxide particles have about one and a half times the mass of air particles.

quiz.p: A bag of water feels almost weightless while it is under water. What is the same idea for air?
opts: A balloon of air seems weightless in air
quiz.why: The water around the bag holds it up. The air around a balloon of air holds it up in the same way. Both the water and the air have mass.

opts: The name of a weather app
Tiny solid and liquid bits floating in air
quiz.why: PM2.5 is not a gas. It is bits smaller than 2.5 thousandths of a millimetre, small enough to reach deep into the lungs.

quiz.p: Two balloons of different gases are compared, but one balloon is bigger. Why is the test not fair?
opts: Two things differ, so the cause is unclear
A fair test needs three balloons
The balloons must be the same colour
quiz.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. If the gas and the size both differ, either could explain the result.

applications: Cooking gas is compressed into a liquid, so that 14.2 kilograms fit in one home cylinder. Buses and autos carry natural gas compressed to about 200 times the pressure of the air.
Packets of chips are filled with nitrogen. It keeps out the oxygen that would turn the oil stale, and it cushions the chips.
Hospitals store oxygen in cylinders and tanks, and give it to people who cannot take in enough from the air.
Some fire extinguishers pour out carbon dioxide. It is heavier than air, so it settles over the fire and keeps oxygen away.
Weather offices in India send up hydrogen-filled balloons every day to measure the air high above the ground.
Anna Mani, a physicist from Kerala, built instruments for India's weather service. One of them measures ozone gas high in the atmosphere.
The Air Quality Index lets a city warn people on days when they should not exercise outdoors.
Divers and firefighters carry compressed air in tanks, so that a small tank holds enough for many breaths.

open_questions.q: How many states of matter are there?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists keep finding new ones in very cold or very squeezed matter. They do not agree on how to count them.

Glass is a liquid that cooled into a solid without its particles lining up in rows. Why it stops flowing is still not fully explained. Some physicists call it one of the hardest unsolved problems about solids.

open_questions.q: Where does the Earth's air end?
open_questions.why_open: The air thins out slowly for hundreds of kilometres and has no edge. Countries and scientists do not agree on a single height for the start of space.

open_questions.q: Is any amount of PM2.5 safe to breathe?
open_questions.why_open: In 2021 the World Health Organization lowered its guideline, because harm was found at lower levels than before. Nobody has yet found a level with no harm at all.

open_questions.q: How will the mix of gases in the air change over the next hundred years?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on how much carbon dioxide people add, and on how much the seas and forests take up. Both are hard to predict.

maths.problem: In Two Balloons on a Hanger, the gas balloon held 2.5 litres. A litre of carbon dioxide has a mass of 1.8 g and a litre of air 1.2 g. How much heavier was the gas balloon than an air balloon of the same size?
maths.explain: Each litre of carbon dioxide is 1.8 − 1.2 = 0.6 g heavier than a litre of air. For 2.5 litres, 0.6 × 2.5 = 1.5 g. That is about 3 small paper clips.
maths.context: This is about Two Balloons on a Hanger. In it, a balloon of carbon dioxide hung lower than an air balloon of the same size.

chart.title: Mass of one litre of three gases

maths.why_maths: The hanger shows only that one balloon is heavier. The sum tells you how much heavier it should be, so you can check it against your paper clips.

maths.problem: A cylinder has 15.3 kg painted inside its top ring. A full one holds 14.2 kg of gas. On a scale it shows 22.4 kg. How much gas is left, and is the cylinder more or less than half full?
maths.answer: 7.1 kg of gas is left. That is exactly half.
maths.explain: Gas left = 22.4 − 15.3 = 7.1 kg. Half of 14.2 kg is 7.1 kg. So the cylinder is exactly half full.
maths.context: This is about Read the Cylinder, where you found the mass of the empty cylinder painted on it.
maths.why_maths: Nobody can see into a steel cylinder. Subtracting the painted number from the scale reading is the only way to know how much gas is left.

maths.problem: You breathe about 6 litres of air every minute. A litre of air has a mass of 1.2 g. About what mass of air do you breathe in one day?
maths.explain: A day has 24 × 60 = 1,440 minutes. 6 × 1,440 = 8,640 litres. 8,640 × 1.2 g = 10,368 g, which is about 10 kg.
maths.context: This is about How Much Gas Is One Breath? In it, you measured the volume of your own breath with an upturned bottle.
maths.why_maths: One breath is too light to feel. Multiplying shows that the air you breathe in a day weighs more than all your food and drink.

maths.problem: In Bean Gas, one bean has 1 chance in 4 of being in the START quarter. For two beans to be there together, the chance is 1 in 16. For three, it is 1 in 64. What is it for all six?
maths.explain: Each extra bean multiplies the number by 4. So: 4, 16, 64, 256, 1,024, 4,096. With six beans, they are all in the START quarter once in about 4,096 looks.
maths.context: This is about Bean Gas, the dice game where six beans spread out over a board and stayed spread.
maths.why_maths: The pattern shows why a gas never gathers in one corner. Six beans almost never gather. A room holds far more particles than six.

maths.problem: In Coins on the Floor, each steam particle sat 12 coin-widths from the next. Real particles spread in three directions: along, across and up. How many times as much space does steam take as water? How much steam comes from 5 ml of water?
maths.answer: About 1,700 times. So 5 ml of water makes about 8.5 litres of steam.
maths.explain: 12 × 12 × 12 = 1,728, which is about 1,700. Then 5 ml × 1,700 = 8,500 ml, or 8.5 litres.
maths.context: This is about Coins on the Floor, where coins stood for the particles of water and of steam.
maths.why_maths: On the floor you could show only two directions. Multiplying three times gives the real change in volume, which is far bigger than it looks on the floor.

maths.problem: In 100 Grains of Air, 4 particles in every 10,000 are carbon dioxide. How many particles of air come with each one particle of carbon dioxide? About what fraction of the air is oxygen, at 21 in 100?
maths.answer: 2,500 particles for each one of carbon dioxide. Oxygen is about one-fifth of the air.
maths.explain: 10,000 ÷ 4 = 2,500. For oxygen, 21 in 100 is close to 20 in 100, and 20 in 100 is one-fifth.
maths.context: This is about 100 Grains of Air. In it, grains of rice and dal stood for the particles of the gases in air.
maths.why_maths: Numbers like 4 in 10,000 are hard to picture. Turning them into 'one in 2,500' tells you how much rice to pour for one clove.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that air is a mixture of gases, each with its own mass? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: For about two thousand years, most scholars in Europe and West Asia held that air was one simple thing. They called it one of the four elements, with earth, water and fire. In 1638 Galileo Galilei forced extra air into a glass flask and weighed it. The flask was heavier, so air has weight. Around the same time, Jan Baptist van Helmont, a doctor near Brussels, wrote that he burned 62 pounds of charcoal. Only 1 pound of ash was left. He said the rest had left as something like air, and he gave it a new name, gas. In the 1750s Joseph Black in Scotland heated a white powder. It lost more than half its mass as a gas. Flames went out in this gas, so it was not ordinary air. In 1766 Henry Cavendish weighed another gas and found it about eleven times lighter than air. In 1894 Lord Rayleigh weighed nitrogen taken from air and nitrogen made from chemicals. The nitrogen from air was heavier, by about 1 part in 200. He and William Ramsay hunted for the reason. They found a gas nobody had noticed, argon.
how_we_found_out.who: Galileo Galilei in Italy, Jan Baptist van Helmont in Brussels, Joseph Black in Scotland, Henry Cavendish, Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay in England
how_we_found_out.when: Galileo's weighing was printed in 1638 and van Helmont's book in 1648. Black worked in the 1750s and Cavendish in 1766. Argon was found in 1894.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That air is one simple element, and that every kind of 'air' is the same thing. Black showed that the gas from his powder put out flames. Cavendish and Rayleigh showed, by weighing, that different gases have different masses.

playtest: Reasoned through step by step, as a parent and child in a city flat would do it. Not yet tried at home. Two Balloons on a Hanger (core) needs balloons, vinegar, baking soda, a one-litre bottle and a coat hanger. The carbon dioxide balloon should be 1 to 2 grams heavier than an air balloon of the same size. That tips a light hanger by 1 to 3 centimetres. A fan or an open window hides this, so the room must be still. Foam in the balloon spoils the result, so the soda goes in slowly. The air balloon against a flat balloon should hardly move the hanger, and it may dip a few millimetres. Weigh the Fizz needs a kitchen scale that shows single grams, and expects a loss of 2 to 4 grams. Use only a fizzy-drink bottle for its closed test. Still Air or Fan gives very different times in different rooms, so the steps say to write what really happens. Pour Air Upwards takes two or three tries. Smoke in Two Jars needs a grown-up and an open window. How Much Gas Is One Breath? works best with a flexible tube, and a strong child may empty the two-litre bottle. Bean Gas usually takes 8 to 26 rounds, about ten minutes. Five Sticky Squares shows only specks big enough to see, so the AQI is recorded beside it. Catch the Gas and Measure It needs a grown-up to make a hole in a bottle cap. Its seal may leak the first time. No part needs a garden.
